Acknowledgements

The Bangsamoro Investment Roadmap Development (BIRD) 2026–2035 has been shaped by analytical work, institutional knowledge, technical exchange and the perspectives of people and organisations working across the Bangsamoro economy. The roadmap is offered as a shared planning resource: its value depends on the continued stewardship, validation and implementation of the institutions and communities it is intended to serve.

Appreciation is extended to the leadership of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) and the Ministry of Trade, Investments and Tourism (MTIT) for providing the institutional setting for investment strategy and coordination. Particular recognition is due to the Bureau of Investments team for its investment-facilitation mandate, working knowledge of the investor environment and continued engagement with the roadmap’s strategic and operational questions.

The work also acknowledges the contributions of officials, technical personnel and practitioners across BARMM ministries, offices and agencies; provincial, city and municipal local government executives and teams; national government agencies; statistical and planning institutions; chambers of commerce, business associations, investors and entrepreneurs; MSMEs and producer organisations; development agencies and financing partners; universities, researchers and training institutions; civil society organisations; and community representatives. Their respective perspectives help connect regional ambition with the practical realities of service delivery, enterprise development, infrastructure, finance, market access, environmental stewardship and inclusive growth.

Gratitude is extended to participants in the structured workshops and consultations convened at regional, provincial, local and sectoral levels. Their discussions and critical reflections have helped test assumptions, surface implementation barriers and highlight the interdependencies that a systems-led roadmap must address. The contribution of the BIRD Validation Survey participants is also acknowledged. The survey provides diagnostic and validation evidence; it is not treated as a population-representative vote or a replacement for authoritative administrative and statistical baselines.

Engr. Addie T. Message from Chief Minister of BARMM

Office of the Chief Minister

Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao

Bismillāhir-Raḥmānir-Raḥīm. The Bangsamoro Investment Roadmap Development (BIRD) 2026–2035 presents a shared direction for translating the gains of peace and autonomy into dignified livelihoods and lasting economic opportunity. Guided by the values of amanah (trust), adl (justice) and stewardship, development must be judged not only by the capital attracted, but by the lives strengthened and the opportunities opened to our people.

Our provinces, island communities and cities possess young talent, productive land and seas, cultural knowledge and a strategic position within wider regional markets. These strengths can generate broader prosperity when linked to reliable infrastructure, capable institutions, responsible investment, access to finance and fair opportunities for local enterprises.

Such a task calls for cooperation across government, local communities, national institutions, the private sector and development partners. The roadmap offers a common framework, while the choices and priorities of the Bangsamoro people must remain central to implementation. May our collective effort serve the public good, protect the trust placed in our institutions and contribute to a peaceful, resilient and prosperous Bangsamoro.

Abdulraof “Sammy Gambar” Macacua

Message from the Minister, MTIT

Ministry of Trade, Investments and Tourism (MTIT)

Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao

The BIRD 2026–2035 positions trade, investment promotion and tourism as connected drivers of enterprise growth and regional competitiveness. For MTIT, the practical challenge is to convert the region’s comparative strengths into credible opportunities that investors can assess, enterprises can join and communities can benefit from.

This calls for more than promotion alone. Investor services, standards, business development, halal value chains, tourism readiness, market intelligence, aftercare and coordination with infrastructure and finance must work as one facilitation system. MSMEs should be able to enter value chains, improve quality and reach markets, while investors receive clear information and predictable, lawful processes.

MTIT’s contribution is to help connect policy direction with business realities: build the investment pipeline, work with partners to resolve barriers, support responsible enterprise and measure results transparently. The roadmap provides a basis for coordination; specific programmes and commitments remain subject to institutional review, financing and approval.

Farsernina A. Mohammad
Minister, Ministry of Trade, Investments and Tourism

Message from the Director General, MTIT

Ministry of Trade, Investments and Tourism

Directorate and operational coordination

The value of BIRD lies in turning a strategic direction into a practical system of responsibilities, work plans and review. The Balanced Scorecard links staff capability and institutional processes with investor and community outcomes and, ultimately, economic performance. For the directorate, this means clarifying who owns each action, which office provides the evidence, where a decision is required and how performance will be reviewed.

Sound execution also requires honesty about what is known. Baselines need source-owner verification; targets must be defined and approved; project readiness, budget execution and physical progress must be distinguished; and material variances require diagnosis before corrective action. The proposed BIF-Net can support shared visibility and coordination, but it must respect legal mandates, data-governance rules and the authority of each participating institution.

Institutional discipline is not administrative overhead. It is part of investor confidence and public accountability. A reliable management system can help the region learn from implementation, direct resources towards binding constraints and connect investment activity with demonstrable development value.

Rosslaini Alonto-Sinarimbo
Director General, MTIT

Glossary of Terms

Adaptive managementUsing monitoring, feedback, learning and governed recalibration to respond to changing implementation conditions.
Bankable projectA project supported by a credible business or public-service case, feasibility work, financing pathway, safeguards, legal approvals, implementation capacity and evidence of demand.
BIMP-EAGAThe Brunei Darussalam–Indonesia–Malaysia–Philippines East ASEAN Growth Area, a regional cooperation initiative for connectivity and economic links.
Balanced Scorecard (BSC)The management architecture that translates the strategy map into four linked perspectives: Financial, Stakeholder, Internal Process, and Learning and Growth.
Bangsamoro Economic and Investment Ecosystem (BEIE)The BIRD framework that organises economic activity into five interdependent clusters (Foundations, Transformers, Enablers, Connectors and Financiers) governed by cross-cutting operating systems.
BIF-NetThe proposed Bangsamoro Investment Facilitation Network: a coordination layer for investment information, investor support, action tracking and performance visibility. It does not replace statutory agency mandates.
Catalytic capitalPublic funds deployed to enable or attract additional investment. The BIRD ₱120–160 billion envelope is indicative; the leverage ratio is a planning objective, not a secured commitment.
Evidence provenanceThe documented source, owner, reference period, geography, definition, calculation, revision history and validation status of a reported value.
Critical Leverage Point (CLP)A high-impact intervention point identified through systems analysis. BIRD uses five: halal certification integrity; the infrastructure, energy and connectivity nexus; governance and investor confidence; the Islamic finance ecosystem; and green economy revenue.
Green Lane statusPriority facilitation for qualified strategic investments, granted by the investment council under the proposed BIF-Net Executive Order.
Implementation frameworkThe three-phase sequence for delivery: Phase 1 Foundation Building (2026–2028), Phase 2 Acceleration (2029–2031) and Phase 3 Consolidation and Global Integration (2032–2035).
Incremental capital-output ratio (ICOR)The investment needed to add one unit of output. BIRD applies 3.5 to 4.0 to estimate the total investment the growth path requires.

Glossary of Terms

Integrated Ecosystem Development Strategy (IEDS)The recommended strategy, aligning investment, production, infrastructure, finance, market access and governance across the BEIE rather than optimising one sector.
Investment approvalA formal approval recorded by the relevant authority; it is not equivalent to cash disbursed, capital realised, a project completed or jobs sustained.
Key performance indicator (KPI)A defined measure used to track progress against an approved objective, with a stated owner, formula, unit, period, source and validation method.
Monitoring, evaluation and learning (MEL)A systematic process for tracking delivery and outcomes, assessing what explains results, and using evidence to improve decisions and implementation.
Investment roadmapA decision and coordination framework that links strategy, facilitation, programmes, financing, implementation and performance management. It does not replace feasibility studies, appropriations or statutory approvals.
Moral governanceA cross-cutting operating principle emphasising transparency, accountability, ethical conduct and institutional integrity in investment and public administration, aligned with Bangsamoro governance values.
MSMEMicro, small and medium enterprise; size classification should follow the relevant official standard and dataset.
Public–private partnership (PPP)A contractual arrangement between the public sector and a private party for eligible infrastructure or services, subject to legal approval, risk analysis and procurement requirements.
Pareto-style headline KPIOne of six high-signal indicators chosen for executive monitoring. The term is a management designation; it does not claim that six indicators cause a fixed share of impact.
Special Geographic Area (SGA)The 63 barangays in North Cotabato that voted to join BARMM, organised into eight municipalities.
Strategy mapA causal diagram showing how Learning and Growth capabilities enable internal processes, which create stakeholder value and contribute to financial outcomes. Links are hypotheses to test, not proof of causation.
Value chainThe linked activities through which inputs are transformed into products or services and delivered to markets or end users.
Systems archetypeA recurring pattern of system behaviour, such as Limits to Growth, Fixes that Fail, Tragedy of the Commons, Growth and Underinvestment, or Shifting the Burden.
TOWS matrixA tool that pairs strengths and weaknesses with opportunities and threats to generate SO, WO, ST and WT strategies.

Executive Summary

From investment potential to shared prosperity

The Bangsamoro Investment Roadmap Development (BIRD) 2026–2035 sets out a coordinated strategy to help BARMM turn its human, cultural, natural and geographic strengths into productive investment, decent work and resilient communities. It matters now because the region must convert the gains of peace and autonomy into durable economic opportunity while addressing poverty, weak connectivity, infrastructure gaps, limited market access and fragmented investment-enabling systems.

BARMM is uniquely positioned to build value across halal products and services, agro-industrial production, the green economy, tourism, trade and Islamic finance. Its location within the Brunei Darussalam–Indonesia–Malaysia–Philippines East ASEAN Growth Area (BIMP-EAGA) provides a platform for wider regional connections—provided that logistics, skills, standards, finance and institutions develop together. BIRD therefore recommends an ecosystem approach rather than isolated sector initiatives.

The roadmap is a strategic and coordination framework, not an approved budget or a guarantee of results. It links the diagnosis in Chapter 2, the Integrated Ecosystem Development Strategy (IEDS) selected in Chapter 3, the calibrated measures in Chapter 4, the Balanced Scorecard (BSC) in Chapter 5, implementation in Chapter 6 and policy recommendations in Chapter 7. Its promise depends on accountable leadership, responsible investment, community participation and transparent, evidence-led execution.

₱120–160BIndicative public catalytic envelope, 2026–2035
₱0.99–1.13TEstimated total investment requirement; scenario, not committed pipeline
₱550B+Proposed BARMM GRDP ambition by 2035; verify price basis and territorial series
76Consented BIRD Validation Survey responses, August 2026
Decision message. Adopt the integrated direction as a basis for coordinated planning; verify all baseline definitions and target series with authoritative data owners; prepare bankable, safeguarded projects; and release public catalytic resources through phase gates tied to readiness, delivery and measurable outcomes.

The Development Challenge

Opportunities and constraints must be addressed together

Chapter 2 frames BARMM’s investment economy as five connected clusters: Foundations, Transformers, Enablers, Connectors and Financiers. The system has real assets—young people, agriculture and fisheries, halal enterprise potential, renewable and natural resources, tourism and strategic regional location—but benefits are constrained when infrastructure, standards, market access, finance, skills and public-sector coordination do not develop in step.

Opportunity–risk matrix

Connect regional strengths to investable, inclusive growth

People and enterprise

Opportunity: a youthful population, entrepreneurs, MSMEs and producer communities can deepen local value chains.

Risk: skills, productivity, access to finance and decent-work pathways may not keep pace with labour-force growth.

Halal economy

Opportunity: build trusted halal value chains, services, certification and market access rooted in Bangsamoro identity and enterprise.

Risk: fragmented standards, limited conformity-assessment capacity and weak traceability could constrain market recognition.

Location and connectivity

Opportunity: deepen trade, logistics, tourism and business links through BIMP-EAGA and wider regional corridors.

Risk: ports, roads, inter-island links, energy reliability and digital connectivity raise costs and limit dependable access.

Natural assets and green value

Opportunity: raise value in agriculture, fisheries, forestry, renewable energy and eligible ecosystem services.

Risk: climate hazards, ecosystem degradation, weak project preparation and uncertain revenue pathways threaten returns.

Investment climate

Opportunity: clearer facilitation, aftercare, investment intelligence and ethical governance can improve confidence.

Risk: fragmented responsibilities, administrative barriers, uncertain readiness and limited coordination slow conversion from interest to operating investment.

Poverty and inclusion

Opportunity: value-chain investment can expand jobs, household income and market participation across provinces and communities.

Risk: poverty, market-access limitations and territorial disparities can prevent growth from becoming broad-based.

What the diagnostics imply

Chapter 2’s systems diagnostics caution against treating each constraint in isolation. Enablers—including infrastructure, energy, digital systems, skills and service delivery—are critical because they influence the performance of the other clusters. The report’s survey analysis found institutional readiness to be the lowest of three assessed dimensions in each of the six survey clusters. This is diagnostic survey evidence, not a substitute for formal agency capacity assessments.

Implication for decisions. Pair productive investments with their dependencies: project preparation, infrastructure and energy, standards and certification, trained people, finance, logistics, buyer demand, climate and conflict-sensitive safeguards, and clear institutional accountability. Where a prerequisite is missing, mark the project accordingly rather than treating it as investment-ready.

Evidence basis: Chapter 2 diagnostics and the BIRD Validation Survey (3–20 August 2026; 76 consented responses). Survey results should be read in light of the sample’s composition and geographic coverage; they are not population-representative estimates.

Strategic Options

Four choices were assessed; an integrated approach ranked first

Chapter 3 assessed four strategic options. Each offers a useful emphasis, but the decision was which approach could address the connected constraints of BARMM’s investment ecosystem rather than improve one sector while leaving binding dependencies unresolved.

Why IEDS was selected

Evaluation logicThe weighted assessment considered economic impact (20%), feasibility (18%), risk–return (16%), identity alignment (15%), systems leverage (15%), inclusivity (10%) and sustainability (6%). The criteria assess complementary aspects of strategic fit and implementation prospects.
Systems leverageIEDS links the five BEIE clusters and addresses cross-cutting operating conditions: moral governance, resilience, inclusivity, and peace and security. It sequences interventions around dependencies rather than assuming sector growth will occur independently.
Stakeholder validationSurvey respondents’ mean ratings also placed IEDS first: 6.05, compared with 5.90 for HEDS, 5.77 for IFES and 5.73 for GEMS among respondents with valid ratings for all options (n=75).
Interpretation disciplineThe separate survey comparison supports further consideration of IEDS; it does not convert the sample into a public referendum or prove that the strategy will cause the projected results.

Critical leverage points

  1. Halal certification integrity: build credible standards, conformity assessment and traceability.
  2. Infrastructure, energy and connectivity: reduce the costs and uncertainty that constrain productive activity.
  3. Governance and investor confidence: clarify decision rights, publish service standards and improve aftercare.
  4. Islamic finance ecosystem: connect Shariah-compliant financing and risk-sharing to viable enterprise and investment needs.
  5. Green-economy revenue: pursue lawful and technically credible mechanisms with environmental safeguards and fair benefit-sharing.
Recommended decision. Use IEDS as the integrating strategy, while retaining the specific contributions of HEDS, IFES and GEMS as mutually reinforcing growth engines. Implement through readiness-based phases and test causal assumptions through MEL.

BSC: Strategy and Investment Roadmap

The Balanced Scorecard translates IEDS into linked objectives, measures, initiatives and review routines. The causal logic runs from Learning and Growth to Internal Process, then to Stakeholder outcomes and Financial results. The four perspectives are interdependent; weights shown in Chapter 5 are proposed management weights and do not replace the definitions and validation rules in Chapter 4.

Performance discipline. Distinguish investment approvals from realised investment, announced jobs from sustained jobs, certificate counts from active valid certificates, and budget execution from physical completion. Assign every KPI an owner, definition, unit, baseline year, territorial coverage, reporting cycle, validation source and a record of revisions.

From objectives to portfolio execution

Each strategic measure should connect to an identifiable programme, activity or project (PAP), with a responsible owner, dependencies, financing status, safeguards, timetable and verifiable milestones. The scorecard is a management tool: it supports decisions and learning but does not prove causal effects merely because indicators move together.

The BIRD Growth Strategy

The growth strategy connects the BEIE clusters and five strategic growth engines through a common investment logic: build enabling conditions, strengthen productive value chains, connect firms to finance and markets, and govern delivery through evidence and accountability. The engines reinforce one another; they are not competing standalone strategies.

1. Halal EconomyStrengthen certification integrity, standards, traceability, compliant processing, skills and access to regional and international markets. Link MSME support to buyer requirements and verified demand.
2. Agro-Industrial DevelopmentIncrease value addition in agriculture, fisheries and other eligible local products through storage, cold chain, processing, quality systems, producer organisation and resilient supply chains.
3. Green EconomyDevelop renewable energy, sustainable production and lawful ecosystem-service opportunities where technical integrity, environmental safeguards, community participation and benefit-sharing are demonstrable.
4. Infrastructure and ConnectivityPrioritise enabling investments in energy, transport, logistics, digital connectivity and climate-resilient infrastructure that remove binding constraints on productive activity.
5. Islamic Finance and Investment PromotionImprove access to Shariah-compliant finance, risk-sharing and capital mobilisation through regulated institutions; strengthen investor intelligence, facilitation, aftercare and project readiness.
One integrated systemAll five engines depend on ethical governance, skills, market demand, reliable data and coordinated implementation. Their contribution should be measured by real outcomes, not activity counts alone.
Delivery principle. Prioritise projects by readiness, developmental contribution, risk, climate and conflict sensitivity, local value capture, market potential and public affordability. No sector label alone makes a project bankable or eligible for public support.

These figures are strategic ambitions in the current report, not independently verified forecasts or adopted statutory targets. Chapter 4’s calibrated headline indicators additionally include 5,000+ halal-certified MSMEs, a household electrification ambition of 90% by 2035 and broadband connectivity of 85%, with indicator definitions and baselines subject to source-owner verification. Renewable-energy share, access to electricity and investment approvals are different measures and must not be conflated.

Three-phase implementation roadmap

Phase 1 — Activate and establish foundations (2026–2028) · ₱35–45B indicative

Purpose: remove binding constraints and establish credible delivery conditions.

Priorities: institutional and legal coordination; verified baselines; project preparation; investor service and aftercare; halal standards readiness; priority energy, transport and digital dependencies; capability and safeguards.

Expected outcome: a validated PAP pipeline, clear ownership, reliable reporting and projects that meet documented readiness gates.

Phase 2 — Scale productive value chains (2029–2031) · ₱50–65B indicative

Purpose: scale investment only when enabling conditions, demand and project viability are verified.

Priorities: agro-industrial processing, halal value chains, cold chain and logistics, green-economy pilots that meet requirements, Islamic finance, export readiness and market links.

Expected outcome: more productive enterprises, better market access and measurable value addition from projects that demonstrate performance.

Phase 3 — Consolidate and integrate globally (2032–2035) · ₱35–50B indicative

Purpose: deepen proven capability and embed institutional continuity.

Priorities: higher-value exports, reliable cross-border market links, institutionalised facilitation, sound green revenue pathways, financial inclusion and independent outcome review.

Expected outcome: stronger economic resilience, a more competitive investment ecosystem and a successor agenda shaped by evaluation findings.

Phase-date consistency. This document uses the canonical Chapter 6 sequencing: 2026–2028, 2029–2031 and 2032–2035. Phase boundaries should be changed only through a controlled cross-chapter revision.

The report’s ₱120–160 billion public catalytic envelope is indicative and phased at ₱35–45 billion, ₱50–65 billion and ₱35–50 billion. The wider ₱0.99–1.13 trillion requirement is derived from an assumed capital-output ratio of 3.5–4.0 and the five-province path to ₱550B (Table 7.6); it is not a list of committed projects, a forecast with guaranteed returns or an approved financing package. The report’s indicative financing scenario allocates potential sources across BARMM public resources, national programmes, development and climate finance, and private, PPP and Islamic finance. Monitoring, evaluation and learning (MEL)

MEL links strategy to implementation and institutional learning. It should report not only money spent and activities completed, but also whether the programme is removing constraints, changing service quality, increasing productive capacity and delivering outcomes. The BSC gives decision-makers a causal structure; Chapter 4 defines indicators and calibration; Chapter 6 specifies reviews and controls; Chapter 7 addresses policy and institutional continuity.

Measure→Learn→Adapt→Improve→Scale
Core MEL discipline
StepManagement questionEvidence and response
MeasureWhat has changed against the approved baseline and target?Verified KPI and PAP records, provenance, date, territory and definition.
LearnWhat explains the change or variance?Root-cause analysis of delivery, finance, dependency, data quality and external shocks.
AdaptWhich response is justified and by whom?Options appraisal, impact on other perspectives, legal authority and stakeholder considerations.
ImproveWas the corrective action implemented and effective?Named owner, due date, decision log and follow-up verification.
ScaleIs the intervention effective, affordable, lawful and replicable?Evidence of outcomes, costs, safeguards and readiness before scale-up decisions.

Illustrative review cadence in Chapter 6: monthly operational pipeline review where data allow; quarterly KPI and delivery review; twice-yearly cross-cluster and territorial review; annual performance and investment programming; a 2030 mid-term review; and a 2035 terminal evaluation.

Data integrity rule. Keep official statistics, administrative records, stakeholder survey findings and management targets distinguishable. Correlation is not proof of causation. Where evidence is unavailable, publish the gap and assign responsibility for closing it.

Why This Matters

What success should look like in 2035

Success is not a single headline number. It is a Bangsamoro investment ecosystem in which enterprises can grow, public institutions can deliver, communities participate in the gains of development, and the economy becomes more diversified and resilient.

Prosperous communitiesMore decent and sustained work, higher local value capture, stronger MSMEs and wider access to productive opportunity across provinces, islands and municipalities.
Competitive industriesHalal and agro-industrial enterprises that meet standards, add value locally, connect to reliable logistics and win repeat business in domestic and international markets.
Ethical and accountable governanceTransparent facilitation, clear decision rights, lawful public spending, credible data and effective routes to resolve investor and community concerns.
A resilient economyInfrastructure and production systems better able to absorb climate and market shocks, with natural assets managed for long-term public and community benefit.
Inclusive developmentWomen, young people, Indigenous Peoples, conflict-affected communities and underserved localities have fairer routes into skills, finance, enterprise and decent employment.
Investment leadershipA reputation built on dependable information, project readiness, responsible investors, effective aftercare and measurable results—not promotional claims alone.

The decisions that matter now

  1. Confirm institutional ownership. Agree decision rights, coordination arrangements and roles for MTIT–Bureau of Investments, participating agencies and local government partners.
  2. Validate the evidence base. Reconcile territorial and price bases; confirm baselines, definitions, source owners and target approval status.
  3. Prepare bankable investments. Prioritise feasibility, demand, finance, safeguards, resilience, local value creation and implementation capacity.
  4. Sequence public catalytic support. Make later releases contingent on readiness and verified performance, with transparent records of funding status.
  5. Review and learn publicly. Publish progress, limitations, corrective action and evaluation findings to sustain trust and improve the next decisions.

The ambition for 2035 is a Bangsamoro where ethical leadership, responsible investment and local ingenuity reinforce one another—where growth is not only larger, but more inclusive, more resilient and more widely shared.

Introduction — Background, Purpose, Anchors and Methodology

A. Background and Rationale: From Post-Conflict Recovery to Investment Destination

The Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) was formally established on 26 February 2019, following the ratification of the Bangsamoro Organic Law (Republic Act No. 11054, 2018) in the plebiscite held earlier that year. The region is more than an administrative reorganisation. It is a political settlement that seeks to turn decades of armed conflict into a durable framework for self-governance, cultural affirmation and economic self-determination.

The region enters the roadmap period with clear evidence of progress and of continuing constraints. On the first-semester measure, poverty incidence among families fell from 55.9 percent in 2018 to 34.8 percent in 2023 (PSA, 2023). On the full-year measure, it fell from 28.0 percent in 2021 to 23.5 percent in 2023, still among the highest of all regions (PSA, 2024). The improvement is substantial, but poverty remains a central development constraint.

The economy is growing again after a slow 2024. Gross Regional Domestic Product (GRDP) grew 2.7 percent in 2024, after 4.3 percent in 2023. In 2024, services accounted for 42.0 percent of GRDP; agriculture, forestry and fishing for 32.4 percent; and industry for 25.6 percent (PSA-RSSO BARMM, 2025). Growth then accelerated to 5.0 percent in 2025, the sixth fastest of the country's 18 regions (MindaNews, 2026). This structure means that value addition, infrastructure, market access, human capital and finance have to be considered together rather than as separate sector programmes.

Investment activity is also rising. Investment approvals reached ₱5.1 billion in the first four months of 2026 (BBOI, 2026). Approvals, however, are not the same as realised capital formation or broad investor confidence. BIRD therefore treats investor confidence as an outcome to be measured through administrative and market indicators, not inferred from a single approval figure.

Provincial trajectories differ. Lanao del Sur was the fastest-growing province in 2023, at 5.02 percent, and grew 4.0 percent in 2024, supported by the SPDA Agro-Industrial Development Program and anchor investments such as DoleFil's ₱306 million pineapple facility. Maguindanao del Norte grew fastest in 2024, at 4.1 percent, on the strength of a services-led economy and growing industrial capacity (MFBM, 2025). Basilan was declared free of the Abu Sayyaf Group on 9 June 2025, a milestone that improves the conditions for normal investment activity (PIA, 2025).

BIRD 2026–2035 · Chapter 1Page 2
Chapter 1

The Bangsamoro Investment Roadmap Development (BIRD) 2026–2035 is MTIT's ten-year strategic framework for investment-led, inclusive and sustainable economic transformation. It builds on the region's productive assets and institutional context: agriculture and fisheries, halal identity and enterprise, a strategic position in BIMP-EAGA, renewable-energy resources, cultural assets, human capital and emerging Islamic finance. The roadmap does not assume that comparative advantage automatically becomes investment advantage. It focuses on the enabling conditions, linkages and execution capabilities needed to turn assets into investable opportunities and broad-based economic outcomes.

B. Scope, Coverage and Temporal Horizon

B.1 Geographic Scope

The roadmap covers BARMM as now constituted: five provinces (Lanao del Sur, Maguindanao del Norte, Maguindanao del Sur, Basilan excluding Isabela City, and Tawi-Tawi), the Special Geographic Area (SGA) and Cotabato City. Sulu has been outside BARMM since the Supreme Court decision of 9 September 2024 (Supreme Court of the Philippines, 2024). Cotabato City, the regional seat of government and the main commercial centre, is treated as a distinct urban node. Each province is profiled through the Bangsamoro Economic and Investment Ecosystem (BEIE) Framework to analyse sectoral linkages and identify priority investment corridors.

Note on official series. Some official statistics, including those for 2023 and earlier, describe the region before Sulu's exclusion. Chapter 4 sets out how baselines are verified and rebased to the current territory before targets are tracked.

B.2 Sectoral Coverage

The roadmap addresses six priority investment sectors, the same six used in the stakeholder workshops, together with the green economy as an emerging cross-cutting pillar. Each is mapped to the BEIE Framework's five functional clusters.

C. Purpose of the Investment Roadmap Development

The BIRD 2026–2035 translates the Bangsamoro Government's investment-promotion mandate into a coherent, evidence-informed roadmap. It connects policy, investment facilitation, sector development, infrastructure, finance, market access and implementation governance, so that individual projects contribute to a functioning investment ecosystem. The roadmap is a decision and coordination framework. It does not replace project feasibility studies, statutory approvals, annual appropriations or agency mandates.

The roadmap serves five related purposes:

1. Integrated analytical framework. Provide a research-based, policy-oriented framework that combines provincial insight, global trends, workshop outputs and multi-sector analysis, kept ecosystem-based by the BEIE Framework and Strat Planner Pro.

2. Evidence-based strategic guidance. Guide policymakers, planners and investors over the decade with strategies grounded in verified PSA-BARMM data, stakeholder evidence and international benchmarks (OIC/SMIIC, ESG, PDP 2023–2028).

3. High-leverage opportunity identification. Identify the investment opportunities and interventions where a small change at the right point produces a large, system-wide effect (Meadows, 1999).

4. Measurable target architecture. Set measurable targets and monitoring mechanisms aligned with international standards, national priorities and Bangsamoro objectives, operated through the Balanced Scorecard and the MEL Dashboard.

5. Synchronised ecosystem development. Replace scattered, siloed interventions with synchronised development, using TOWS and systems archetypes so that strategies reinforce one another across clusters.

D. Guiding Principles

Six guiding principles shape analysis, strategy, implementation and learning. They work as operating rules for investment facilitation and public decision-making. Where they carry measurable indicators, targets remain subject to baseline verification and periodic calibration.

Principle 1: Moral Governance
Transparency, accountability and Islamic ethics (khalifa) are the operating system of investment facilitation. Facilitation processes are subject to public disclosure, investor-protection mechanisms and anti-corruption safeguards. Operational metric: 100 percent public procurement disclosure by 2028; investor ombudsman operational by 2027.
Principle 2: Ecosystem Thinking
Sectors are treated as interconnected clusters, not isolated silos. Every provincial plan maps inter-cluster linkages explicitly, because treating connected sectors in isolation produces inefficiency and missed opportunities (Silva, 2026a).
BIRD 2026–2035 · Chapter 1Page 5
Chapter 1
Principle 3: Cultural Authenticity
Bangsamoro identity, including halal, Islamic finance and Maranao, Maguindanaon, Iranun, Yakan and Sama heritage, is a genuine competitive advantage. This principle guides halal certification, Islamic finance and cultural tourism. Operational metric: 5,000+ halal-certified MSMEs and an SMIIC mutual recognition arrangement by 2035.
Principle 4: Environmental Stewardship
Green economy pathways, carbon markets and nature-based solutions are economic opportunities, not compliance costs. This principle drives Forestry Code implementation, REDD+ development and payments for ecosystem services. Operational metric: ₱500M+ annual green revenue by 2035; renewable share of generation kept at or above the BSEMP baseline of 75.86 percent.
Principle 5: Inclusivity
Investment benefits must reach MSMEs, farming and fishing communities, women, youth and internally displaced persons, through MSME-focused promotion, livelihoods linked to anchor investments and gender-responsive project design. Operational metric: 60 percent+ MSME participation in value chains; poverty below 20 percent by 2035.
Principle 6: Data-Driven Decision-Making
Strategies rest on verified economic data and stakeholder evidence, through PSA-BARMM data integration, synthesis of workshop outputs and KPI benchmarking. Operational metric: quarterly BIF-Net and MEL Dashboard updates; annual independent evaluation.

E. Regulatory and Policy Anchors

The BIRD 2026–2035 operates within a legal and policy framework that spans three tiers: national legislation, BARMM-specific instruments, and regional and international frameworks. These anchors align the roadmap with national priorities, international standards and the region's autonomous governance structure.

E.1 National Legislation and Issuances

Bangsamoro Organic Law (Republic Act No. 11054, 2018). The BOL establishes BARMM's autonomous government and directs it to promote investment and create a favourable climate for business in the region (Article XIII, Section 24). It provides the legal basis for region-specific policies on investment facilitation, halal development and economic zones, within the Constitution and applicable national laws.

CREATE MORE Act (Republic Act No. 12066, 2024). CREATE MORE sets the national fiscal incentive framework that applies to registered enterprises in BARMM: income tax holidays, the special corporate income tax, the enhanced deductions regime, duty and VAT incentives, and the RBE local tax. Its enhanced deductions for research and development, training, power and domestic inputs directly support the Enablers and Transformers clusters.

2026 Strategic Investment Priority Plan (Memorandum Order No. 47). The SIPP defines the activities eligible for incentives nationwide. It includes area-specific priority activities for BARMM, namely halal tourism and investment operations of Islamic banks under RA 11439 (Office of the President, 2026). Widening this BARMM list is a policy objective of the roadmap (Chapter 7).

Islamic Banking Law (Republic Act No. 11439, 2019). The law provides the framework for Islamic banks and Shariah-compliant financial services. The Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas licenses and supervises Islamic banks; the Bangsamoro Government's role is to build demand, project pipelines, Shariah-governance capacity and public-sector use of Islamic instruments.

Republic Act No. 11550 (2021). The law divided the former Maguindanao province into Maguindanao del Norte and Maguindanao del Sur, enabling province-specific investment strategies.

E.2 BARMM-Specific Legal and Policy Instruments

2nd Bangsamoro Development Plan (BDP) 2023–2028. The BDP sets medium-term development priorities and sectoral targets. It is the primary planning document that the BIRD operationalises through investment facilitation strategies (BPDA, 2023).

Bangsamoro Investment Code (draft). The draft Code, as of 22 April 2026, sets out the regional framework for investment incentives, the roles of investment promotion agencies, an investment development council and non-fiscal support (MTIT, 2026a). Its harmonisation with CREATE MORE and with BIF-Net is addressed in Chapter 7.

Proposed Executive Order on the Bangsamoro Investment Facilitation Network (BIF-Net). The proposed order establishes BIF-Net as the inter-agency investment facilitation framework and creates a Regional Green Lane for Strategic Investments, with MTIT-BoI as permanent secretariat (Office of the Chief Minister, 2026).

BIRD 2026–2035 · Chapter 1Page 7
Chapter 1

Bangsamoro Halal Industry Development Plan (BHIDP) 2025–2030. The BHIDP sets the strategy for the halal ecosystem, certification infrastructure and export market linkages (MTIT-BARMM, 2025). It is the primary operational plan for halal investment in the Transformers cluster.

Bangsamoro Sustainable Energy Master Plan (BSEMP). The BSEMP reports a renewable share of generation of 75.86 percent and sets the pathways for renewable development, grid connection and electrification (MENRE-BARMM, 2024). It anchors energy investments in the Foundations and Enablers clusters.

Bangsamoro Forestry Code (pending). The Code was pending before the interim Parliament's Committee on Environment, Natural Resources and Energy; its enactment now rests with the first elected Parliament. It will set the legal basis for sustainable resource use, value-added forest products and access to environmental markets, including REDD+ and payments for ecosystem services.

Draft MENRE–MILG Joint Memorandum Circular No. 2026-01. The draft circular, for signature, sets frameworks for carbon credit programmes, payments for ecosystem services and eco-tourism user fees as revenue mechanisms for local governments and communities. Its adoption is a Chapter 7 recommendation.

E.3 Regional and International Frameworks

BIMP-EAGA EGL Sub-Committee Strategic Plan 2025–2028. The Brunei Darussalam–Indonesia–Malaysia–Philippines East ASEAN Growth Area (BIMP-EAGA) Environment, Green Economy and Land Use plan provides a regional framework for green economy integration and cross-border trade (BIMP-EAGA, 2024). Tawi-Tawi's proximity to Sabah and the SGA's position on the central Mindanao corridor give BARMM natural trade advantages within the growth area.

Philippine Development Plan (PDP) 2023–2028. The PDP sets national priorities and indicators against which BARMM's contribution is aligned and monitored (NEDA, 2023).

OIC/SMIIC standards. The Standards and Metrology Institute for Islamic Countries (SMIIC) provides the main international framework for halal standards and for the accreditation of halal certification bodies, guiding BARMM's certification infrastructure and market-access strategy (SMIIC, 2021).

ASEAN Economic Community Strategic Plan 2026–2030. Adopted in May 2025 under the ASEAN Community Vision 2045, the plan succeeds the AEC Blueprint 2025 as the regional integration framework that BARMM engages through BIMP-EAGA (ASEAN, 2025).

UN Sustainable Development Goals. The SDGs inform the roadmap's inclusive growth strategies, particularly Goals 1 (no poverty), 8 (decent work and economic growth), 9 (industry, innovation and infrastructure) and 13 (climate action).

F. Analytical Frameworks and Methodology

The BIRD 2026–2035 uses two complementary analytical frameworks, the Bangsamoro Economic and Investment Ecosystem (BEIE) Framework and the Strat Planner Pro Architecture, to provide methodological rigour, systems-level analysis and actionable outputs. This section introduces both frameworks, the five-step methodology that integrates them, and the stakeholder process that supplied much of the evidence.

F.1 The Bangsamoro Economic and Investment Ecosystem (BEIE) Framework

The BEIE Framework moves investment analysis away from isolated sectoral silos towards an integrated view of how economic clusters interact and reinforce one another. Grounded in systems-based economic theory, it organises BARMM's economy into five functional clusters, anchored by moral governance and supported by four cross-cutting enablers: tourism and culture, peace and security, human capital, and environmental sustainability (Silva, 2026a).

The framework's core insight, that BARMM's sectors are deeply interconnected and that treating them in isolation wastes effort and opportunity, is a governance imperative as much as an analytical finding. The five clusters are set out in Figure 1-3 and Table 1-5.

F.2 The Strat Planner Pro Architecture

The Strat Planner Pro Architecture (Silva, 2026b) provides the planning and roadmapping architecture for the BIRD 2026–2035. It integrates five analytical layers, namely SWOT analysis, systems thinking and mapping, the strategy matrix, metrics and KPI benchmarking, and the Balanced Scorecard, so that diagnosis becomes measurable, time-bound implementation.

Tool 1: SWOT analysis with quantified indices. Strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats are identified with stakeholder attribution and variable classification, then scored with a distinct formula for each quadrant (see Chapter 2 for the full diagnostic).

SWOT formulas
• RIStrengths = (Impact × Likelihood) / 5 — scale 0.2–5, resilience capacity
• RIOpportunities = √(Impact × Likelihood) — scale 1–5, resilience through exploitation
• RiskWeaknesses = Impact × Likelihood — scale 1–25, internal risk exposure
• VIThreats = (Impact² × Likelihood) / 25 — scale 0.04–5, external vulnerability

Tool 2: Systems thinking and systems mapping. Causal loop diagrams map reinforcing and balancing feedback loops. Systems archetype analysis identifies recurring patterns such as Limits to Growth, Fixes that Fail, Shifting the Burden and Tragedy of the Commons that determine where intervention has the most leverage (Senge, 1990; see Chapter 2).

Tool 3: Strategy matrix (TOWS). The TOWS matrix matches internal strengths and weaknesses with external opportunities and threats to generate SO, WO, ST and WT strategies. Each strategic option is evaluated with a seven-criteria weighted scoring matrix (see Chapter 3).

BIRD 2026–2035 · Chapter 1Page 12
Chapter 1

Tool 4: Metrics benchmarking and KPI calibration. Strategic objectives are translated into KPIs with baselines, targets and data sources, benchmarked against international standards (OIC/SMIIC, ESG, SDGs), national targets (PDP 2023–2028) and Bangsamoro objectives (see Chapter 4).

Tool 5: Balanced Scorecard (BSC). The BSC translates strategy into measurable outcomes across four perspectives (Financial, Stakeholder, Internal Process, and Learning and Growth), linking capability investments to economic and inclusion outcomes. The scorecard is developed in Chapter 5; implementation, annual programming and MEL in Chapter 6; and policy and institutional recommendations in Chapter 7.

Evidence, measurement and governance contract. The roadmap distinguishes three evidence layers: (1) official administrative and statistical baselines; (2) stakeholder-validation evidence; and (3) analytical assumptions used for scenario development. The BIRD validation snapshot contains 76 consented survey responses, analysed under analyticsVersion 2. Survey-derived SWOT diagnostics use the canonical formulas above, as implemented in the validation-survey analytics service. Missing SWOT answers are reported as missing observations, not zeros. Survey diagnostics support prioritisation and learning; they do not establish official baselines or targets. Chapter 4 governs KPI calibration; Chapters 5 and 6 translate calibrated measures into scorecard and implementation systems; Chapter 7 sets the policy and institutional conditions for sustained execution.

F.4 Stakeholder Engagement and Workshop Process

The BIRD 2026–2035 was built from the ground up. It started with regional working sessions, moved through the provinces, and was then checked through a region-wide validation survey. At each stage the Strat Planner Pro Framework's participatory data-collection method guided the work. Participants did not only comment on a draft: they wrote the problem statements, opportunities, priorities and pathways that the roadmap analyses. The process ran in five stages (Figure 1-6).

Stage 1: Regional workshops (January–February 2026)

Two rounds of regional workshops brought together representatives of Bangsamoro ministries, offices and agencies (BMOAs), the private sector (small and medium enterprises and major businesses) and development partners. Working in sector groups, participants applied five Strat Planner Pro tools in sequence to six investment sectors: agro-industry, halal, tourism, energy and utilities, infrastructure, and services. Each tool took the previous tool's output as its input (Table 1-7).

Table 1-7. Workshop tools and outputs
WorkshopGuiding questionWhat participants produced
1. Sectoral challengesWhat holds investment back in each sector, and why?Problem statements (what, where, who), effects on the sector, root causes and supporting evidence
2. Sectoral opportunitiesHow can each challenge become an opportunity for joint action?Opportunity and investment areas, possible programmes, partner institutions and time horizons
3. Opportunity prioritisationWhich opportunities should come first?Opportunities placed on an impact-and-feasibility matrix (Do first, Plan and advocate, Nice to have, Park), with the top three to five presented in plenary and justified by impact and feasibility
4. Industry SWOTWhat are each industry's strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats?A structured SWOT for each sector
5. Industry strategyWhat is the pathway from today's situation to the desired outcome?A description of the current situation, three sequenced milestones and expected outcomes for each sector
BIRD 2026–2035 · Chapter 1Page 15
Chapter 1

Stage 2: Mainland provincial workshop, Cotabato City (24 March 2026)

The process then moved to the provinces. On 24 March 2026, a workshop in Cotabato City brought together BMOAs, local government units (LGUs) and private-sector participants from Maguindanao del Norte, Maguindanao del Sur and the Special Geographic Area (SGA). It used the same participatory method to test the regional findings against provincial conditions.

Stage 3: Provincial workshops with BEIE cluster conversations (May–June 2026)

On 12 May 2026, a provincial workshop for Lanao del Sur was held in Marawi City. On 20 June 2026, the MTIT Basilan Provincial Office organised a consultative workshop for Basilan in Isabela City, which lies outside BARMM; the discussion covered the BARMM part of the province. The Basilan Economic and Investment Outlook served as the visual guide, and participants accepted all of its data and insights. Both sessions strengthened the method in two ways:

  • discussion was organised around the clusters of the Bangsamoro Economic and Investment Ecosystem (BEIE), so participants looked at how sectors depend on one another rather than treating each in isolation;
  • each workshop started from a prepared Provincial Economic and Investment Outlook, which gave participants a shared base of data and context before they began (MTIT, 2026b).

Both workshops drew a wide range of government, LGU and private-sector stakeholders.

Every province consulted in person. All five provinces and the SGA took part in a provincial workshop: Maguindanao del Norte, Maguindanao del Sur and the SGA in Cotabato City (24 March 2026), Lanao del Sur in Marawi City (12 May 2026), Basilan at a consultative workshop organised by the MTIT Basilan Provincial Office in Isabela City (20 June 2026), where participants accepted all data and insights in the Basilan Economic and Investment Outlook, and Tawi-Tawi in Bongao (28 October 2026), where participants validated the Tawi-Tawi Economic and Investment Outlook (results).

Stage 4: Validation survey (3–20 August 2026)

The BIRD Validation Survey tested the workshop findings and the roadmap's draft logic with a wider audience. All 76 responses carry final consent under the Data Privacy Act of 2012. The online survey drew no responses from Basilan or Tawi-Tawi; the two island provinces were validated in person, Basilan at its June workshop and Tawi-Tawi at its October validation (BIRD Validation Survey, 2026).

BIRD 2026–2035 · Chapter 1Page 16
Chapter 1

From participation to analysis

The planning team synthesised the workshop outputs and survey responses through the Strat Planner Pro architecture:

  • quantified SWOT scoring;
  • causal loop diagrams and systems archetypes;
  • leverage-point analysis;
  • the TOWS strategy matrix;
  • the Balanced Scorecard.

The team then formulated the four strategic options and scored them against seven weighted criteria, which led to the recommended Integrated Ecosystem Development Strategy (IEDS). Findings were cross-checked against PSA-BARMM data, the provincial economic and investment outlooks, and relevant national and international benchmarks.

The roadmap therefore combines three kinds of evidence: official statistics, stakeholder evidence and systems analysis. Each is kept distinct. Where evidence is incomplete or may change, the roadmap marks the item for baseline verification, feasibility assessment or later calibration rather than presenting an assumption as fact.

Context, BEIE Framework and Integrated Strategic Diagnostics

From Environmental Scanning to Systems Sensing

A conventional environmental scan lists political, economic, social, environmental and technological factors one after another. That is useful but incomplete, because in BARMM these factors do not act separately. A drought in Maguindanao del Sur is an environmental event, but it becomes an economic shock to processors, a fiscal pressure on local governments and a social strain on farming households within one season. This chapter therefore uses the Bangsamoro Economic and Investment Ecosystem (BEIE) Framework as a living systems lens: it asks not only what is happening in each domain, but where each force acts within the economy and how it travels between clusters (Silva, 2026).

Deep presencing means sensing both the visible and the emergent: the data and trends, and also the relationships, feedback loops, institutional habits and cultural currents that produce them (Senge, 1990; Meadows, 2008). The chapter moves from context (Sections 2.1 and 2.2), through a quantified diagnosis of the cross-cutting operating systems and the five clusters (Sections A to F), to a synthesis of how the clusters behave as one system (Section G).

BIRD 2026–2035 · Chapter 2Page 2
Chapter 2
How evidence is used in this chapter. Three kinds of evidence are kept distinct: official statistics (PSA and other data owners), stakeholder evidence (the workshops and the BIRD Validation Survey, n = 76 consented responses) and analytical synthesis. Survey scores show how stakeholders judge conditions; they are not official baselines. Where a figure is an estimate from the BIRD KPI register, it is labelled as such.

The PEDSET–BEIE lens

The six PEDSET domains (political, economic, demographic, social, environmental and technological) are mapped to the clusters where they actually operate. Table 2-1 is the reading key for the rest of the chapter: each cluster section begins with the PEDSET signals that matter most for that cluster, and Section G traces how those signals cross cluster boundaries.

Table 2-1. Where PEDSET forces act within the BEIE clusters
PEDSET domainPrimary point of actionHow the force travels across clusters
PoliticalCross-cutting operating systems (moral governance, peace)Governance credibility and security set the risk premium for every cluster; policy continuity decides whether incentives in Transformers and Financiers are believed.
EconomicAll five clustersPrices, demand and capital flow from Foundations through Transformers to Connectors; Financiers determine how fast the cycle turns.
DemographicEnablers (human capital)A young, fast-growing population is a labour supply for Transformers and a consumer market for Connectors only if Enablers convert it into skills.
SocialEnablers; Connectors; operating systems (inclusivity)Poverty, literacy and trust shape productivity, market depth and the social licence for investment.
EnvironmentalFoundations; operating systems (resilience)Climate shocks and resource degradation start in Foundations and pass into processing, logistics and credit risk.
TechnologicalEnablers (digital, infrastructure); ConnectorsConnectivity and digital public services lower transaction costs everywhere; their absence caps the scale of every other cluster.
The systems question. For each force, the chapter asks three things: where it lands first, which cluster it reaches next, and whether the resulting loop reinforces investment or holds it back. The answers, taken together, identify the binding constraint on the whole system (Section G).

2.1 Global Economic Trends: Implications for BARMM

The global outlook is steady but fragile. The International Monetary Fund projects world growth of 3.1 percent in 2026 and 3.4 percent in 2027 (IMF, 2026). For BARMM, the external environment matters less through headline growth than through specific channels: the price of food, fuel and fertiliser; the direction of regional supply chains; the availability of climate and Islamic finance; and the pace of digital change. Table 2-2 sets out each trend and the cluster through which it enters the regional economy.

Table 2-2. Global trends and their entry points into the BEIE clusters
TrendGlobal contextImplication for BARMM (entry cluster)
Moderate global growthWorld growth of about 3 percent, with downside risks from trade tensions and geopolitical uncertainty (IMF, 2026).Export demand for agricultural, fisheries and halal products may soften; domestic consumption and public investment must carry more of the growth (Connectors).
Supply-chain realignmentTrade is shifting towards regional supply chains, including within ASEAN.BIMP-EAGA corridors and ecozones become more valuable as alternative routes and production sites (Connectors, Transformers).
Commodity price volatilityFood, fuel and fertiliser prices remain exposed to climate and geopolitical shocks.Higher input costs hit farm margins and diesel-dependent island power (Foundations, Enablers).
Digital transformation and AIInvestment in digital infrastructure, e-government and AI-driven productivity is accelerating.Without broadband and digital skills, BARMM risks a widening productivity gap; the Bangsamoro e-Governance Master Plan is the main response (Enablers).
Climate adaptation financeMultilateral and climate funds are expanding finance for resilience and green infrastructure.Renewable energy, coastal protection and climate-smart agriculture can attract concessional finance if projects are prepared (Foundations, Financiers).
Islamic finance growthIslamic banking, sukuk and takaful continue to grow globally.A culturally aligned source of capital for infrastructure and MSMEs, if domestic institutions and pipelines are ready (Financiers).
Changing labour marketsAutomation and AI are changing the skills that employers need.Skills systems must move faster to match investor demand (Enablers).

These trends reinforce one message. BARMM's exposure to the global economy runs mostly through its Foundations and Connectors clusters, while its capacity to respond sits in Enablers and Financiers. Resilience to external shocks is therefore an outcome of cluster coordination, not of any single sector policy.

BIRD 2026–2035 · Chapter 2Page 4

2.2 Regional Economic Trajectory: Indicators and Inflection Points

BARMM's trajectory shows real progress on three fronts: output, investment and poverty (Figure 2-2). Growth slowed to 2.7 percent in 2024, after 4.3 percent in 2023 and 6.6 percent in 2022 (PSA-RSSO BARMM, 2024, 2025a), then recovered to 5.0 percent in 2025, the sixth fastest of the country's 18 regions (MindaNews, 2026). Investment approvals have accelerated, and poverty has fallen sharply since 2018.

Approvals are a signal of intent, not of capital on the ground. They have also been volatile: ₱6.97 billion was approved in 2021, followed by lower totals before the recent rise (MTIT, 2026a). The roadmap therefore tracks realised investment, jobs and retention alongside approvals (Chapter 4).

Economic structure

The structure of the economy explains why value is lost between clusters. Agriculture, forestry and fishing (AFF) generate about a third of regional output, roughly four times their share nationally (about 8 percent), yet most of that output leaves the region unprocessed (Figure 2-3). The gap between a large Foundations cluster and a small Transformers cluster is the clearest structural signal in the regional accounts.

Inflection points

Governance transition. The first regular Bangsamoro Parliament was elected on 14 September 2026, with turnout of about 80 percent. No party won a majority, so the Chief Minister will be chosen through coalition when members take office after 30 October 2026 (Reuters, 2026). A peaceful election strengthens governance credibility; a contested coalition process would test it. The campaign also saw an ambush on the interim Chief Minister on 15 August 2026, who survived the attack (Daily Tribune, 2026), a reminder that political stability still needs active protection.

Security normalisation. Basilan was declared free of the Abu Sayyaf Group on 9 June 2025 (PIA, 2025). For investors, this lowers the risk premium in a province with large rubber and aquaculture endowments and a ₱6.67 billion power interconnection project under way (MTIT, 2026b).

Quantified SWOT and Systems Mapping Within the BEIE Clusters

Sections A to F diagnose the cross-cutting operating systems and the five clusters in the same way: (1) the PEDSET signals that act on the cluster; (2) stakeholder-scored SWOT evidence from the validation survey; (3) the systems archetype that best describes the cluster's behaviour; and (4) the investment and institutional response. Table 2-5 brings the quantified evidence together on one page.

Scoring method. Each SWOT item was rated for Impact (1–5) and Likelihood (1–5) and scored with the canonical BIRD formulas: Strength RI = (I × L) / 5; Opportunity RI = √(I × L); Weakness Risk = I × L (scale 1–25); Threat VI = (I² × L) / 25. Cluster values are the means across all valid item ratings. Where the survey asked no questions for a SWOT family in a cluster, the value is shown as n/a and is not treated as zero. Readiness and urgency are separate 1–5 ratings of each cluster as a whole.

Three readings stand out. First, Enablers carries the heaviest internal risk and the widest gap between urgency and readiness (0.71 points), which marks it as the binding cluster. Second, opportunity scores are consistently high (3.93–4.04 out of 5): stakeholders do not doubt that opportunities exist. Third, readiness is the lowest of the three cluster ratings everywhere; the constraint is institutional throughput, not a shortage of assets. Section G shows how these readings combine.

A. Cross-Cutting Operating Systems: Moral Governance, Resilience, Inclusivity and Peace

A.1 Functional Descriptions and Deep Presencing Indicators

The BEIE Framework treats moral governance, resilience, inclusivity and peace as the operating systems of the economy, not as aspirations. As an operating system manages how hardware and software interact, these four systems govern the trust, incentives and accountability through which value is created in every cluster (Silva, 2026). The political domain of PEDSET acts mainly here, together with the social and environmental domains through inclusivity and resilience.

The workshops repeatedly identified three bottlenecks: fragmented programme delivery across Bangsamoro ministries, offices and agencies (BMOAs); weak inter-agency coordination that produces duplication and gaps; and investor hesitation rooted in perceptions of governance and security risk. These are not sectoral failures. They are operating-system failures, and they call for changes in rules, information flows and institutional design rather than more sector programmes (Meadows, 1999; BoI-MTIT, 2026).

Table 2-6. Cross-cutting operating systems: functions, indicators and imperatives
Operating systemFunctionDeep presencing indicatorsInvestment and policy imperative
Moral governanceTransparency, accountability, stability, Islamic ethics and the rule of law as the basis of investment facilitationBudget execution; public disclosure of incentives; investor-protection mechanisms; integrity of halal certificationInstitutionalise an investor ombudsman; publish procurement data; pair incentives with institutional milestones
ResilienceAbsorbing climate and economic shocks; food, water and infrastructure securityDrought and flood losses; pest and disease early warning; value-chain diversification; contingency financeScreen all infrastructure and agro-investments for climate risk; adopt continuity and adaptive-management protocols
InclusivityFair sharing of benefits; MSME integration; opportunity for women, youth and internally displaced personsMSME participation in value chains; sex-disaggregated employment; financial inclusion by municipalityLink anchor investments to local sourcing; scale Islamic microfinance and waqf; target skills programmes at excluded groups
PeaceSecurity, conflict prevention, normalisation and narrative managementSecurity incidents; investor perception; reconciliation coverage; return of displaced personsSustain normalisation; publish security and investment data; fund community-led peacebuilding

A set of regional plans and instruments in the BIRD evidence base gives the operating systems an institutional backbone. Several are still drafts or pending, which is itself a governance signal: the rules that would let the operating systems work are not yet all in place (Table 2-7).

A.3 Political Domain: Governance Credibility and Security Stability

The political domain shapes the investment climate through three channels: governance credibility, policy continuity and security. The validation survey shows that stakeholders see these channels as the region's most serious external threats (Table 2-8). Security incidents carry the highest vulnerability index of any threat in the survey, ahead of climate change.

Table 2-8. Political and governance threats as rated by stakeholders
ThreatThreat VI (0–5)Clusters most exposedWhat it signals

Drifting goals3.03Operating systemsTargets may be quietly lowered unless they are governed

BIRD 2026–2035 · Chapter 2Page 10
Chapter 2

Security risk is uneven across the region. Clan feuds (rido), residual armed groups and disputes over land and resources are the main drivers on the mainland; maritime insecurity and smuggling are concerns in the island provinces. These patterns are monitored by the security sector and independent conflict monitors, and the roadmap uses them as risk signals rather than as fixed ratings. The most effective response is to keep normalisation programmes funded, invest in community-led peacebuilding and publish security and investment data together, so that improvements reach investors as evidence rather than as assertion.

Basilan illustrates the peace–investment link. Its declaration as free of the Abu Sayyaf Group on 9 June 2025 came as the ₱6.67 billion Zamboanga–Basilan Interconnection Project and major public works were advancing in the province (PIA, 2025; MTIT, 2026b). Security, power and logistics improvements reinforce one another; none of them alone would attract processing investment.

A.4 Environmental and Geophysical Hazards

The provinces, the Special Geographic Area and Cotabato City face earthquakes, flooding, landslides, storm surges and drought. Climate change is the second-highest-rated threat in the survey (VI 3.14), and the evidence shows it is already a present cost: El Niño-induced drought led Maguindanao del Sur to declare a state of calamity in 2024, with ₱346 million in crop losses across 1,370 hectares, and Pestalotiopsis leaf disease has infested at least 800 hectares of Basilan's rubber (MTIT, 2026b).

The policy implication runs across clusters. Climate-resilient agriculture (drought-tolerant varieties, water management and diversified cropping) belongs in Foundations; climate-risk screening and resilient design belong in Enablers; and takaful and contingency finance belong in Financiers. Treating these as separate programmes would leave the shock free to pass between them.

A.5 Deep Presencing Insight: Applying the Iceberg Model

The operating systems must be strengthened first. Incentives offered without parallel governance reform can produce short-term approvals but not lasting transformation. The Iceberg Model explains why: visible events are produced by deeper patterns, structures and mental models (Senge, 1990; Meadows, 1999). Stakeholders strongly endorsed this reading: 85 percent agreed that the Iceberg Model describes BARMM's investment system, with a mean rating of 4.26 out of 5 (BIRD Validation Survey, 2026).

Level 1: Events (what is happening?)
Visible outcomes that trigger immediate responses: approvals rising to ₱5.1 billion in January–April 2026; capital that arrives with incentive announcements and leaves when incentive periods end; budget execution below 80 percent. Reacting only to events treats symptoms.
Level 2: Patterns (what keeps recurring?)
Investment surges followed by slowdowns; persistent gaps between policy announcement and implementation; recurring delays in procurement, certification and aftercare. Isolated interventions produce temporary gains without changing the trajectory.
BIRD 2026–2035 · Chapter 2Page 12
Chapter 2
Level 3: Structures (what produces the patterns?)
Incentives decoupled from institutional capacity; programme delivery fragmented across BMOAs; no real-time system linking governance performance to investment outcomes; weak feedback from investor experience to policy. Structures decide whether incentives compound into growth or dissipate through friction.
Level 4: Mental models (what beliefs hold the system in place?)
The belief that fiscal incentives alone attract quality investment; the assumption that governance reform can follow production rather than precede it; the view that sectors work independently; and the habit of measuring success by approvals rather than retention, impact and inclusion. Shifting from "incentives first" to "governance first" changes the whole strategy.
Table 2-10. Iceberg monitoring framework for the operating systems

The lesson is that strengthening the operating systems first is an investment imperative, not a governance preference. Working only on events (approvals and incentives) without changing structures and mental models will keep reproducing the boom-and-bust cycle. Stakeholders were divided on how realistic this is: 36 percent rated moral governance "very realistic" as an operating system, but the largest group (39 percent) said it "needs stronger institutional support".

Systems archetype and leverage response

Archetype: Fixes that Fail. Quick fixes such as incentives without capacity milestones relieve pressure briefly, then produce side-effects (dependency, capital flight, eroded trust) that recreate the original problem. 96 percent of respondents judged this an accurate description (37 percent "very accurately").

B. Cluster 1: Foundations — Agriculture, Fisheries, Forestry, Energy and Environment

The Foundations cluster is the resource base on which the rest of the economy depends. It feeds raw materials to Transformers and commodities to Connectors, so it sits upstream of almost all value creation. AFF accounts for 32.4 percent of regional output, and the region's energy mix is predominantly renewable, led by the Agus hydropower cascade in Lanao del Sur (PSA-RSSO BARMM, 2025a; MENRE-BARMM, 2024).

PEDSET signals in this cluster. Environmental: drought, floods and crop disease. Economic: volatile commodity and input prices. Political: land tenure and resource governance. Technological: low farm mechanisation and post-harvest technology.

B.2 Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry: The Living Resource Base

Agro-industry is the region's most strategic and most under-performing sector. Production remains concentrated in low-value primary goods, with limited processing, weak market links and high post-harvest losses. Anchor investments show what is possible: DoleFil's ₱306 million pineapple packing plant in Wao began commercial operation in 2022 and employs more than 1,200 people, and Green Arrow Agri-Ventures' foreign-owned project in Amai Manabilang, under the SPDA programme, is projected to create 499 jobs (MTIT, 2026b).

Climate and disease are already testing the base. AFF output contracted 4.2 percent in 2024 (PSA-RSSO BARMM, 2025a), as El Niño drought hit Maguindanao del Sur and Pestalotiopsis spread through Basilan's rubber. The provinces' endowments differ sharply (Figures 2-6 and 2-7; Table 2-12), so a single regional programme would fit none of them well.

B.3 Energy and Environmental Systems: Powering and Protecting the Base

Reliable, affordable power is the single most important enabling condition for industrial investment. The generation mix is predominantly renewable, but access is not: about 40 percent of potential household connections in BARMM electric cooperative areas were energised in 2023 (NEA, 2023), and region-wide household electrification stood at 67.52 percent at the end of 2025 (Context.ph, 2026). Island provinces rely heavily on diesel, which raises costs for processors. Workshop 1 identified three core energy problems: an unreliable power industry with ailing electric cooperatives; insufficient electrification in island and remote barangays; and unused renewable and non-renewable potential (BoI-MTIT, 2026). The devolution of power-sector functions from the DOE to MENRE, agreed in 2026, gives the region new tools and new responsibilities (Context.ph, 2026).

C. Cluster 2: Transformers — Industry, Manufacturing, Logistics and Halal Processing

The Transformers cluster is the value-adding engine: the processing and manufacturing capacity that turns Foundation materials into market-ready products. It decides whether BARMM captures value within its borders or exports it as unprocessed commodities. Industry accounts for 25.6 percent of regional output (PSA-RSSO BARMM, 2025a), and manufacturing in Maguindanao del Norte grew 27 percent between 2018 and 2023 (MTIT, 2026b).

PEDSET signals in this cluster. Economic: scale, input costs and access to buyers. Political: halal certification governance and standards recognition. Technological: cold chain, quality laboratories and traceability. Social: cultural legitimacy of Bangsamoro halal products.

• Halal certification processing time: 45–60 days (target ≤21 days by 2035; BIRD KPI register)

D. Cluster 3: Enablers — Infrastructure, Social Services and Protection, Health and Human Capital

The Enablers cluster is the physical, digital and human infrastructure that makes value creation possible. Without reliable power, transport, connectivity and skills, Foundations cannot reach Transformers and Transformers cannot reach Connectors. The quantified evidence identifies Enablers as the binding constraint: it has the highest weakness risk (17.13 out of 25), the lowest readiness (3.33) and the highest urgency (4.04) of all clusters (Table 2-5).

PEDSET signals in this cluster. Demographic: a young, fast-growing population. Social: poverty, literacy and malnutrition. Technological: broadband gaps and digital public services. Economic: infrastructure cost overruns and budget execution.

The human-capital gap is acute. In 2024, 81.0 percent of residents had basic literacy, the lowest of any region (national: 90.0 percent), and 64.7 percent were functionally literate (national: 70.8 percent) (PSA, 2025; PSA-RSSO BARMM, 2025b). The population is growing about 3.43 percent a year (MTIT, 2026a). That growth becomes a demographic dividend only if education and skills keep pace with what employers need. Workshop 1 identified the skills mismatch, with technical and vocational programmes concentrated in a few oversubscribed qualifications, as a direct barrier to investment (BoI-MTIT, 2026).

E. Cluster 4: Connectors — Tourism, Digital Connectivity, Trade, Exports and BIMP-EAGA Integration

The Connectors cluster is how BARMM's products, services and cultural assets reach markets beyond the region. It determines whether value creation stays local or earns external revenue and multiplier effects. BARMM has a dual gateway: BIMP-EAGA to the south and west, through Tawi-Tawi, about 20 km from Sabah, and the Philippine domestic market to the north, through the mainland and the central Mindanao corridor (MTIT, 2026b). Ports, customs facilitation and digital trade platforms remain underdeveloped.

PEDSET signals in this cluster. Economic: halal market growth and competition from established hubs. Political: cross-border trade rules and security. Technological: logistics and digital trade. Social: cultural heritage as a tourism asset.

F. Cluster 5: Financiers — Islamic Banking, Waqf, Takaful and Microfinance

The Financiers cluster is the capital circulation system for all other clusters. In BARMM it has a distinctive dimension: Shariah-compliant finance fits the values of a predominantly Muslim population of about 4.5 million people, and offers a recognised route to global Islamic capital. Yet formal financial penetration is low, and Islamic banking assets in the region are estimated at below ₱2 billion (BIRD KPI register).

PEDSET signals in this cluster. Economic: MSME credit demand and project bankability. Political: national regulation and regional coordination. Social: religious values and financial literacy. Technological: digital financial services for island and rural users.

Republic Act No. 11439 provides the national framework for Islamic banking. The Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas licenses and supervises Islamic banks; the region's role is to build demand, project pipelines, Shariah-governance capacity and public-sector use of Islamic instruments. The government-owned Al-Amanah Islamic Investment Bank of the Philippines operates in the region, and CARD Islamic Bank has established operations in Marawi City under RA 11439 (MTIT, 2026b). Stakeholders favour macro-capital instruments such as sukuk and infrastructure finance as the first priority (56 percent), and 72 percent consider a coordinating Islamic finance authority essential.
