G. Cross-Cluster Systems Synthesis: From Five Diagnostics to One Investment System

The BEIE Framework's value lies less in describing each cluster than in showing how the clusters interact through reinforcing and balancing loops. These interactions decide whether the ecosystem compounds value or loses it through fragmentation and bottlenecks (Silva, 2026; Senge, 1990).

Cross-cluster systems synthesis

Two Engines of Ecosystem Growth

System sequencing. Foundations supply the productive and ecological base; Enablers lift capacity ceilings; Transformers convert resources into higher-value products; Connectors move them into domestic, ASEAN and global markets; Financiers mobilise capital across the system. The operating systems decide whether these flows are trusted, inclusive, resilient and peaceful.
Integrated investment logic. The evidence supports a sequencing principle rather than five separate sector programmes: secure the resource base → build enabling capacity → scale transformation → connect markets → deepen finance, with governance, resilience, inclusion and peace working at every step.
BIRD 2026–2035 · Chapter 2Page 33
Chapter 2

The throughput reality

Because value passes through the clusters in sequence, readiness gaps multiply rather than average. Table 2-16 makes the arithmetic explicit. Averaged, the clusters look about 69 percent ready; multiplied through the chain, the system converts only about 16 percent of its potential, and about 11.5 percent once the operating systems are applied. The weakest link, Enablers, caps the whole chain.

Table 2-16. From cluster readiness to system throughput
Stage in the value chainReadiness (1–5)As share of 5Cumulative throughput
C1 Foundations3.4569.0%69.0%
C3 Enablers3.3366.6%46.0%
C2 Transformers3.4068.0%31.2%
C4 Connectors3.6172.2%22.6%
C5 Financiers3.5571.0%16.0%
Operating systems (applied to the chain)3.5871.6%11.5%

Source: BIRD Validation Survey (2026), cluster readiness ratings (63–73 valid answers each). The multiplicative model is an illustrative systems heuristic: it assumes each stage passes on only the share of value it is ready to handle. It is not an econometric estimate.

The master reinforcing loop (R6)
Foundations (AFF at 32.4% of GRDP) → Enablers (the ₱6.67B Zamboanga–Basilan Interconnection Project) → Transformers (manufacturing up 27% in Maguindanao del Norte, 2018–2023) → Connectors (BIMP-EAGA and GCC corridors) → Financiers (approvals of ₱5.1B in January–April 2026) → back to Foundations (anchor investors such as DoleFil in Wao sourcing from local farms).

Implication: synchronisation is essential, because weakness at any one point constrains the whole loop. This is the structural case for the Integrated Ecosystem Development Strategy recommended in Chapter 3.
BIRD 2026–2035 · Chapter 2Page 34
Chapter 2

Provincial diagnostics and island–mainland dynamics

The cluster analysis shows an island–mainland divergence. In the island provinces, Basilan and Tawi-Tawi, strong Foundation endowments (rubber, seaweed and fisheries) hit hard Enabler ceilings in power, shipping, connectivity and skills, the Limits to Growth pattern. On the mainland, the main constraint is institutional: interventions produce uneven results because of coordination and capacity gaps, the Fixes that Fail and Shifting the Burden patterns. The Special Geographic Area, with new local governments and unresolved land tenure, needs institutional and infrastructure investment at the same time.

Chapter 3

Strategic Options, Leverage Points and the Roadmap Strategy

Introduction: From Diagnosis to Strategy

Chapter 2 diagnosed the Bangsamoro economy as one connected system. It quantified 55 strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats across the cross-cutting operating systems and the five clusters of the Bangsamoro Economic and Investment Ecosystem (BEIE) Framework; it identified the systems archetypes that keep the region's investment performance below its potential; and it showed that readiness gaps compound along the value chain, so that clusters that look about 69 percent ready on average deliver only about 11.5 percent of their potential as a system. This chapter turns that diagnosis into a strategic choice.

It does so through three analytical layers, each building on the one before:

  1. SWOT-to-strategy conversion (Section A, A.1–A.4). The quantified SWOT register is converted into SO, WO, ST and WT strategies using the TOWS matrix (Weihrich, 1982). Every strategy is traced to scored survey items, the BEIE cluster that owns it and the archetype it addresses.
  2. Systems-archetype-informed leverage points (Section B). Each archetype is mapped to the levels of Donella Meadows' hierarchy of places to intervene in a system (Meadows, 1999), and the results are consolidated into the five Critical Leverage Points (LP1–LP5) used in Chapters 4 to 7.
  3. Multi-criteria evaluation of four strategic options (Section A, A.5–A.7). Halal Economy Dominance (HEDS), Green Economy Monetisation (GEMS), Infrastructure-First Enabling (IFES) and Integrated Ecosystem Development (IEDS) are scored against seven weighted criteria, tested for sensitivity and then compared with stakeholder validation results.
BIRD 2026–2035 · Chapter 3Page 2
Chapter 3
Baseline scores and validation results are reported separately. The option matrix in Section A.6 is an analytical decision aid: its baseline scores are structured expert judgements made with the Strat Planner Pro method. Stakeholder validation results from the BIRD Validation Survey are a second, independent evidence stream and are reported beside the baseline, never blended into it. Where the two agree, confidence rises; where they differ, the difference is reported as a finding.

What Chapter 2 hands to Chapter 3

Table 3-1 lists the diagnostic findings that shape the strategy, and the design requirement each one places on any option the region adopts. These requirements become the tests that the four options must pass in Section A.6.

Section A

Systems-Based Strategy Matrix and Strategic Options

The TOWS matrix (Weihrich, 1982) pairs internal factors (strengths and weaknesses) with external factors (opportunities and threats) to generate four families of strategy. BIRD applies it with three disciplines borrowed from systems thinking. First, only scored items enter the matrix: each pairing uses factors from the BIRD Validation Survey register rather than descriptive lists. Second, each strategy is assigned to the BEIE cluster that owns its delivery, so that the matrix can be read as a map of the ecosystem. Third, each strategy is tagged with the archetype it is designed to weaken and the Meadows level at which it intervenes, which links Section A to Section B.

Scoring conventions. SWOT items use the canonical Strat Planner Pro formulas applied in Chapter 2: Strength Resilience Index (RI) = (I × L) / 5; Opportunity RI = √(I × L); Weakness Risk = I × L on a 1–25 scale; Threat Vulnerability Index (VI) = (I² × L) / 25, where I is impact and L is likelihood, each rated 1–5. The four families therefore sit on different scales and are compared within, not across, families.

Each table gives the paired SWOT items with their scores, the archetype the strategy is designed to weaken, the Meadows level at which it intervenes (L-numbers follow Meadows, 1999, from L12 parameters to L1 transcending paradigms) and the Critical Leverage Point (LP1–LP5) it serves. A.1 SO Strategies: Using Strengths to Capture Opportunities

SO strategies are the growth pathway. They connect the region's strongest scored assets (a large resource base, seaweed and agricultural specialisation, cultural credibility and location) with its highest-rated external opportunities (halal markets, renewable investment and regional integration). They are attractive but conditional: each depends on Enablers that Chapter 2 found to be the weakest cluster.

Table 3-3. SO strategies with leverage-point integration
StrategyStrengths (RI)Opportunities (RI)Archetype addressedMeadows levelCLP
SO-1 Halal and agro-industrial value chainsSeaweed dominance 3.71; AFF base 3.69; Polloc Freeport 3.43; domestic halal demand 3.36; halal legitimacy 3.26Global halal market 4.13; ASEAN halal economy 4.05; UAE corridor 3.92Growth and UnderinvestmentL10 stock-and-flow; L5 rulesLP1
SO-2 Renewable energy and natural-capital monetisationLake Lanao 3.24; renewable endowments 3.15Renewable investment 4.12; PES 3.99; Forestry Code 3.97; carbon markets 3.66Tragedy of the CommonsL5 rules; L4 self-organisation; L6 informationLP5, LP2
SO-3 BIMP-EAGA gateway and Muslim-friendly tourismCultural heritage 3.59; BIMP-EAGA location 3.50BIMP-EAGA integration 4.08; landbridge 4.02; tourism recovery 3.91Success to the SuccessfulL10 stock-and-flow; L5 rulesLP2, LP3

SO-1 is the core of the halal pathway. Its strongest pairing is not halal legitimacy itself, which scores in the middle of the strength register (3.26), but the resource base that halal products are made from: seaweed (3.71) and agriculture, fisheries and forestry (3.69), matched with the highest-rated opportunity in the register, the global halal market (4.13). The constraint is conversion, not supply: Tawi-Tawi exports most of its seaweed raw, and cold chain (16.42) and market linkage (16.41) are among the highest-rated weaknesses. SO-1 therefore intervenes at L10 (processing, testing and cold-chain capacity built ahead of demand) and at L5 (accreditation rules that open export markets), anchored by the Bangsamoro Halal Park in Matanog and agro-industrial corridors in Lanao del Sur and the SGA (MTIT, 2025; MTIT, 2026).

SO-2 converts environmental endowments into revenue through renewable energy, payment for ecosystem services (PES) and, where eligible, carbon markets. Its legal precondition is the Bangsamoro Forestry Code and the joint MENRE–MILG issuance on benefit sharing, both still pending. Without these rules, SO-2 would accelerate the Tragedy of the Commons rather than resolve it. SO-3 uses location and culture to reach BIMP-EAGA and Muslim-friendly tourism markets; it intervenes in physical links (ports, the Mindanao–Sabah landbridge concept, island logistics) and in rules that spread benefits beyond the already-connected mainland.

A.2 WO Strategies: Using Opportunities to Overcome Weaknesses

WO strategies are turnaround initiatives. They matter most in BARMM because the register's highest-risk items are internal: six of the ten highest-rated weaknesses sit in the Enablers cluster. External opportunities, such as concessional climate finance, digital technology and Islamic finance, supply the capital and capability that internal resources alone cannot.

Table 3-4. WO strategies with leverage-point integration
StrategyWeaknesses (Risk)Opportunities (RI)Archetype addressedMeadows levelCLP
WO-1 Infrastructure and energy enablingInfrastructure deficits 17.41; low technology adoption 16.62Renewable investment 4.12; climate-adaptation finance 4.03; digital leapfrogging 4.10Limits to GrowthL10 stock-and-flow; L9 delays; L11 buffersLP2
WO-2 Human-capital transformationLow literacy 18.19; malnutrition 17.84; poverty 17.15; skills mismatch 16.96Digital leapfrogging 4.10; post-conflict reconstruction 3.90Limits to Growth; Fixes that FailL10 stock-and-flow; L3 goalsLP2
WO-3 Cold chain, market linkage and certification capacityCold chain 16.42; market linkages 16.41; halal certification 15.65Global halal market 4.13; ASEAN halal economy 4.05Growth and UnderinvestmentL10 stock-and-flow; L9 delays; L6 informationLP1
WO-4 Islamic financial inclusion for MSMEsFinancial penetration 15.66Islamic finance ecosystem 3.99Shifting the BurdenL4 self-organisation; L5 rulesLP4

WO-1 addresses the physical ceiling on growth. Household electrification reached 67.52 percent region-wide at the end of 2025, against a Bangsamoro Sustainable Energy Master Plan target of 90 percent by 2035 and 100 percent by 2040; broadband coverage is estimated in the BIRD KPI register at below 30 percent (MENRE-BARMM, 2024; Context.ph, 2026). The ₱6.67 billion Zamboanga–Basilan Interconnection Project is the clearest example of a single enabling asset that changes what Basilan can process (MTIT, 2026). WO-1 intervenes mainly at L10 (building the stock of roads, power and connectivity), L9 (shortening project preparation and delivery delays) and L11 (reserve capacity so that new investment does not immediately saturate the grid).

WO-2 addresses the highest-rated risk in the entire register. In 2024 only 64.7 percent of BARMM residents were functionally literate, against 70.8 percent nationally, and basic literacy (81.0 percent) was the lowest of any region (PSA, 2025). Because human capital accumulates slowly, WO-2 must start in Phase 1 even though its returns arrive mainly in Phases 2 and 3; this is the classic delay that makes capacity investment easy to postpone. WO-3 builds the conversion capacity that SO-1 depends on, and WO-4 builds Islamic financial capability (products, providers and financial literacy) rather than relying on one-off conventional or grant financing, the pattern that Chapter 2 identified as Shifting the Burden.

A.3 ST Strategies: Using Strengths to Absorb Threats

ST strategies are protective. They deploy the region's strengths against the threats that could reverse investment gains. The threat register is led by security incidents (VI 3.20), commodity price volatility (3.19) and climate change (3.14), all external pressures that BARMM cannot remove but can buffer.

Table 3-5. ST strategies with leverage-point integration
StrategyStrengths (RI)Threats (VI)Archetype addressedMeadows levelCLP
ST-1 Standards recognition and halal quality assuranceHalal legitimacy 3.26; cultural heritage 3.59Halal hub competition 2.88; standards recognition 2.77Success to the Successful (at international scale)L5 rules; L6 informationLP1
ST-2 Climate-resilient FoundationsAFF base 3.69; renewable endowments 3.15Climate change 3.14; price volatility 3.19; Pestalotiopsis 2.69Fixes that FailL11 buffers; L6 information; L5 rulesLP5, LP2
ST-3 Peace-conditioned investment confidencePeace dividend 3.50; policy recognition 3.45; young population 3.37Security incidents 3.20; political transition 2.85EscalationL8 balancing loops; L6 informationLP3

ST-1 rests on a realistic reading of competition. Established halal hubs in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand have deeper supply chains and recognised certification systems. BARMM's route to premium markets is therefore not price but trust: certification that importing authorities accept, backed by laboratory testing and traceability. This makes accreditation and mutual recognition under OIC/SMIIC standards a critical-path item for the halal pathway rather than a compliance formality (SMIIC, 2021; MTIT, 2025).

ST-2 treats climate risk as a present cost. El Niño-related drought led Maguindanao del Sur to declare a state of calamity in 2024, and Pestalotiopsis leaf disease has affected at least 800 hectares of rubber in Basilan (Chapter 2). The strategy combines buffers (irrigation, crop diversification, climate-resilient varieties), information (early warning and climate-risk screening of projects) and rules (adaptation conditions on subsidies), avoiding relief-only responses that recreate the problem. ST-3 uses the peace dividend, including Basilan's declaration as free of the Abu Sayyaf Group on 9 June 2025 (PIA, 2025), to strengthen the balancing loops that keep isolated incidents from becoming investor-wide risk premiums: rapid incident response, verified security information for investors and protection of project sites.

A.4 WT Strategies: Reducing Weaknesses and Avoiding Threats

WT strategies address the points where internal weakness meets external threat, and where the region is most exposed. They are defensive in form but preventive in purpose: they protect the roadmap itself from the failure modes Chapter 7 identifies, namely being ignored after a change of government, executed in silos or allowed to drift.

Table 3-6. WT strategies with leverage-point integration
StrategyWeaknesses (Risk)Threats (VI)Archetype addressedMeadows levelCLP
WT-1 Delivery, budget execution and data reformUnderspending 16.85; fragmented data 15.75; fragmented policy 15.46Drifting goals 3.03; national coordination 2.91; fragmented mandates 2.57Drifting Goals; Fixes that FailL6 information; L5 rules; L3 goalsLP3
WT-2 Infrastructure cost and delivery assuranceInfrastructure deficits 17.41Cost overruns 3.07; cyber insecurity 2.80Limits to GrowthL9 delays; L8 balancing loopsLP2
WT-3 Land tenure and shared-resource governanceLand tenure 15.92Security incidents 3.20; Pestalotiopsis 2.69Tragedy of the CommonsL5 rules; L4 self-organisationLP5
WT-4 Investment continuity through political transitionFragmented policy 15.46Political transition 2.85; drifting goals 3.03Big Man; Drifting GoalsL3 goals; L5 rules; L2 paradigmLP3

WT-1 is the cheapest source of additional capital in the roadmap. Underspending is rated a high risk (16.85), and every percentage point of budget execution recovered is capital that does not have to be raised. The strategy works through information (one version-controlled baseline and project register, as recommended in Chapter 7, B1), rules (readiness gates and published service standards) and goals (protecting targets from being lowered quietly when performance lags). Respondents rated the Drifting Goals archetype accurate at 98.6 percent, and 30 of 45 who answered the follow-up said both of its loops are equally observable (BIRD Validation Survey, 2026).

WT-2 introduces cost and schedule assurance, because infrastructure cost overruns carry the highest impact rating of any threat (I = 4.28). WT-3 resolves the land-tenure overlaps (ancestral domain claims, private titles and public land) that block agro-industrial siting, with free, prior and informed consent where indigenous peoples' rights apply. WT-4 responds to the first elected Bangsamoro Parliament: the roadmap must be anchored in law, budget rules and published targets so that it outlasts any single administration (Chapter 7, D1).

A.5 Strategic Options Formulation

The fourteen TOWS strategies can be bundled in different ways, and each bundle expresses a different theory of how BARMM's economy should grow. Four coherent options were formulated during the BIRD workshops and tested in the validation survey. The options are not mutually exclusive in content; they differ in emphasis, sequencing and the constraint they treat as binding.

Table 3-7. How the TOWS strategies combine into the four options
OptionTOWS strategies bundledConstraint treated as bindingFailure mode if pursued alone
HEDS Halal Economy DominanceSO-1, WO-3, ST-1Market access and certificationProcessing and export capacity outrun power, logistics and skills; growth stalls at the Enablers ceiling (Growth and Underinvestment becomes Limits to Growth).
GEMS Green Economy MonetisationSO-2, ST-2, WT-3Unpriced natural capitalRevenue depends on legal instruments, measurement systems and buyers not yet in place; green revenue currently stands near zero.
IFES Infrastructure-First EnablingWO-1, WO-2, WT-2Infrastructure and human capitalCapacity is built ahead of conversion; value accumulates upstream with no processing or market link to release it, and political support erodes before returns appear.
IEDS Integrated Ecosystem DevelopmentAll fourteen, sequenced in three phasesThe weakest link in a serial chain, wherever it liesCoordination overload: too many fronts for the available institutional capacity unless a single orchestration function and readiness gates are in place.
BIRD 2026–2035 · Chapter 3Page 10
Chapter 3

Option profiles

Option 1 · Halal Economy Dominance Strategy (HEDS)
Thesis. Use the region's halal legitimacy and resource base to build certified, processed and exported halal products, with the Bangsamoro Halal Park, Polloc Freeport and provincial agro-industrial corridors as anchors. Strengths. The strongest identity fit and the clearest investor narrative. Weakness. It concentrates on the Transformers cluster while the binding constraint lies in Enablers; it also exposes the region to the threat of competition from mature halal hubs (VI 2.88) before certification is internationally accepted.
Option 2 · Green Economy Monetisation Strategy (GEMS)
Thesis. Turn forests, watersheds, marine ecosystems and renewable resources into revenue through renewable energy, PES, eco-tourism and eligible carbon instruments. Strengths. The highest sustainability score and a direct response to the Tragedy of the Commons. Weakness. The thinnest institutional base: the Forestry Code and the benefit-sharing issuance are pending, measurement, reporting and verification (MRV) systems are not yet built, and community safeguards must precede any transaction.
Option 3 · Infrastructure-First Enabling Strategy (IFES)
Thesis. Remove the binding infrastructure, energy and human-capital constraints first, then scale production. Strengths. It targets the cluster that Chapter 2 identified as binding and has high systems leverage. Weakness. It is sequential: by deferring conversion and market capacity, it leaves returns invisible for years, which weakens the political and fiscal case for continuing investment.
Option 4 · Integrated Ecosystem Development Strategy (IEDS)
Thesis. Synchronise the strongest elements of Options 1 to 3 according to their dependencies: Enablers and Foundations are prepared first, Transformers scale as their prerequisites are verified, and Connectors and Financiers deepen as product and project flows grow, with the operating systems working throughout. Strengths. It is the only option consistent with the serial-throughput finding of Chapter 2 and the only one that addresses every diagnosed archetype. Weakness. It is the most demanding to coordinate, which is why its feasibility depends on the orchestration arrangements set out in Chapters 6 and 7.
Why serial throughput favours synchronisation. When value must pass through several clusters in sequence, system output is the product of their readiness levels, not the average. In a product, a one percent improvement in any cluster raises total throughput by about one percent, so no cluster can be safely deferred; and because the absolute gain is largest where readiness is lowest, the weakest link (Enablers) must be raised first. A single-sector option improves one factor of the product and leaves the others unchanged.

Three readings follow. First, IEDS leads on five of the seven criteria and is never ranked below second. Second, each single-sector option leads where its thesis predicts: HEDS on identity alignment, GEMS on sustainability (tied with IEDS) and IFES on systems leverage among the standalone options. Third, the decisive gap is in systems leverage and economic impact, the two criteria that capture whether an option changes the structure of the system, which is precisely what Chapter 2's throughput analysis says is required. The lowest score for IEDS is risk–return (7.5): integration spreads exposure across more fronts, a cost that the phase gates in Section A.7 are designed to manage.

Sensitivity of the ranking

A ranking that changes when the weights change slightly is not a robust basis for a ten-year roadmap (Belton and Stewart, 2002). Table 3-10 re-scores the baseline under alternative weightings and under a stress test that penalises IEDS for its coordination burden.

Reading the validation evidence

The order is fully reproduced; the conviction is not. Stakeholders reproduced the baseline order exactly, in the full sample and in the subset who moved at least one slider. However, their scores are lower and closer together: the IEDS lead over HEDS is 0.15 points in the full sample and 0.22 among slider movers, against 1.30 points in the baseline. At the level of individual respondents, IEDS was the strict first choice of 22 percent of slider movers (32 percent including ties). The baseline should therefore be read as a well-supported direction, not as a decisive margin of stakeholder preference.

Default responses compress the spread. Twenty-five of the 75 respondents who reached the matrix left all 28 cells at the default value of 5. Their answers pull every option towards the midpoint, which is why the slider-mover subset is reported alongside the full sample.

Where stakeholders see it differently. Among slider movers, HEDS outscored IEDS on identity alignment (6.74 against 6.58), and inclusivity was IEDS's strongest criterion (7.06). Stakeholders thus see the integrated strategy as the more inclusive choice and the halal strategy as the more authentic expression of Bangsamoro identity. IEDS should carry the halal agenda visibly, rather than subsume it.

Direct endorsement. Asked whether IEDS should be the overarching strategy, 44 of 65 respondents (67.7 percent) answered yes, 20 (30.8 percent) agreed partially and one asked for more evidence; none rejected it. Survey frame. The survey is a non-probability sample of 76 consented respondents, collected 3–20 August 2026. Of the 72 who named a location, 27 were from Cotabato City, 22 from Maguindanao del Norte, 11 region-wide, 7 from the SGA, 3 from Maguindanao del Sur and 2 from Lanao del Sur; none were from Basilan or Tawi-Tawi. A.7 Recommended Strategy: The Integrated Ecosystem Development Strategy (IEDS)

The Integrated Ecosystem Development Strategy is recommended as the overarching strategy for BIRD 2026–2035. Three arguments support the recommendation, each independent of the others:

  1. Structural fit. The economy behaves as a serial chain whose output is capped by its weakest cluster. Only an option that raises all clusters in dependency order can lift system throughput materially (Chapter 2, Section G).
  2. Archetype coverage. IEDS is the only option that responds to all six cluster archetypes and the three governance archetypes diagnosed in Chapter 2 (Section B.2).
  3. Robustness. IEDS ranks first under every weighting tested and in both stakeholder samples, and was endorsed outright or partially by 64 of 65 respondents.

IEDS does not mean doing everything at once. It means testing each project against the upstream conditions it needs (reliable power and logistics, lawful land access, capable workers, accepted standards, finance, safeguards and credible offtake) and funding those conditions alongside the project where justified. The sequence is implemented through the three phases that Chapter 6 operationalises.

Gates, not dates. A later phase is not authorised because its planned start date has arrived. Each project passes a readiness gate before scale-up (verified scope, owner, financing, safeguards, land access and offtake), consistent with Chapter 6. Phases therefore overlap in practice: a Phase 2 processing investment can proceed in 2027 if its power, land and market prerequisites are already verified.

The budget-priority tension. Asked where budget should concentrate, respondents put Foundations first (29 of 71) and the operating systems second (15), with Enablers fifth (6), even though readiness data identify Enablers as the binding cluster. The two views are reconciled rather than overruled: Enablers investments are selected and justified by the Foundations pipelines they unlock, such as farm-to-market roads, cold chain and power for agro-processing (Chapter 7, B4).

Financing logic and 2035 targets

The ₱120–160 billion envelope is an indicative requirement for public and catalytic finance over the decade, not a single approved budget. Chapter 6 sets out an illustrative financing scenario of 35 percent from BARMM appropriations and other regional public resources, 25 percent from national government programmes, 30 percent from official development assistance and climate finance, and 10 percent from private capital, public–private partnerships and Islamic finance. Stakeholders broadly support blended finance (63 of 72 agree or strongly agree), but rated the fairness of the proposed mix more cautiously (3.68 of 5). Each share must be replaced by verified appropriations or signed commitments as they become available.

Managing the risks of integration

The principal risk of IEDS is the one its feasibility score anticipates: coordination load. Integration multiplies interfaces between ministries, local governments, investors and development partners, and the weakest interface sets the pace. Table 3-14 lists the main risks and the mitigation built into the roadmap.

Table 3-14. Principal risks of the integrated strategy and their mitigation
RiskHow it would showMitigation in the roadmap
Coordination overloadProjects wait for permits and decisions held by different agencies; issues escalate without resolutionOne investment-facilitation network (BIF-Net) with an Orchestration Office in MTIT-BoI for case management, data and aftercare; five BEIE cluster councils (Chapter 7, A2–A3)
Resource dilutionMany small allocations, few completed assetsReadiness gates and a ranked, version-controlled project pipeline (Chapter 6)
Target driftTargets lowered quietly when performance lagsVariance triggers and documented corrective plans; quarterly BSC review (Chapters 5–6)
Political transitionReprioritisation after a change of administrationAnchoring in law and budget rules; policy review calendar to 2035 (Chapter 7, D1)
Territorial concentrationInvestment clusters in the mainland corridorProposed allocation floor for lagging and island areas; provincial investment nodes (Chapter 7, B3)

Stakeholders favoured the same direction. Asked which mitigation mattered most, 45 of 61 chose a single coordination centre for investment delivery (presented in the survey as an investment command centre), ahead of trigger-based budgeting (9), climate finance for green sequencing (5) and a 20 percent contingency reserve (2). Chapter 7 gives this function its institutional form as the BIF-Net Orchestration Office: a coordinating and case-management function, not an additional approving body. On reform sequencing, 42 of 73 respondents preferred institutional, fiscal and regulatory reforms to proceed in parallel.

Section B

Systems Archetype-Informed Strategic Leverage Points

Section A chose the strategy; Section B identifies where, within the system, that strategy should push. A leverage point is a place in a system where a small, well-placed change produces a large and lasting shift in behaviour (Meadows, 1999). Meadows ranked twelve such places from the least to the most powerful, and the hierarchy is used here as a practical diagnostic: for each archetype diagnosed in Chapter 2, it asks which level of intervention would weaken the structure that produces the problem.

Table 3-15. Meadows' hierarchy of leverage points, grouped into four realms
RealmMeadows levelsTypical BIRD intervention
Parameters (shallow; quick to change)L12 constants and numbers; L11 buffers; L10 stock-and-flow structuresIncentive rates, budget amounts, reserve capacity, physical infrastructure
FeedbacksL9 delays; L8 balancing loops; L7 reinforcing loopsFaster approvals and project delivery, rapid-response mechanisms, performance-linked funding
DesignL6 information flows; L5 rules; L4 self-organisationPublished delivery data, accreditation rules, co-management and cluster councils
Intent (deep; slow to change, most durable)L3 goals; L2 paradigms; L1 transcending paradigmsInclusive and stewardship-based goals, a shift from competition to collaboration

Sources: Meadows (1999); the four realms follow Abson et al. (2017).

Three numbering systems, kept distinct. In this report, L1–L12 refer to Meadows' levels; LP1–LP5 are the five Critical Leverage Points (identifiers, not Meadows levels); and the Balanced Scorecard's Learning and Growth objectives in Chapter 5 use separate codes.

B.1 Identifying Leverage Points: A Three-Step Diagnostic Process

Leverage points were identified through a three-step process from the Strat Planner Pro architecture, applied first in the regional and provincial workshops and then tested in the validation survey (Silva, 2026; BoI-MTIT, 2026).

Step 1: Diagnostic synthesis. Recurring patterns are identified from the scored SWOT register and the workshops: production that cannot scale beyond local power and logistics limits; certification and processing capacity that lags demand; shared resources degraded by fragmented governance; investment concentrated in the mainland corridor; and short-term financing that delays durable institutions.

Step 2: Loop mapping. Each pattern is traced to its feedback structure. Chapter 2 mapped the investment–development reinforcing loop and the governance–investor confidence loop (rated accurate by 97 and 91 percent of respondents) and the balancing loops that cap them. The question at this step is where a loop is delayed, broken or dominated by a balancing limit.

Step 3: Tiered selection. Interventions are chosen across realms. Parameter changes are fast but shallow; design and intent changes are slow but durable. A credible portfolio uses both, with deeper interventions protecting the gains of shallower ones. Respondents found the leverage points clear (mean 4.00 of 5; 76.7 percent agree) and agreed that activating them would accelerate the ecosystem (4.03; 79.5 percent).

Chapter 3

Activating leverage points

The archetype map shows a clear pattern. Four levels recur across almost every archetype: L10 (building the stock of physical and human capacity), L6 (making performance visible), L5 (changing the rules that shape behaviour) and L3 (protecting the goals). BARMM's past interventions have concentrated on L12 and L10, through budget amounts, incentive rates and infrastructure projects. These remain necessary, but without the design and intent levels they are vulnerable to Fixes that Fail and Drifting Goals. IEDS therefore pairs every major capital programme with a rule, an information flow and a goal that protect it.

Design principle. No major investment without its protecting rule. For example: a processing facility (L10) is paired with an accreditation pathway (L5) and published certification times (L6); an energy interconnection (L10) with a tariff and dispatch arrangement (L5) and a reliability dashboard (L6); a provincial allocation (L12) with an equity floor (L5) and a provincial disparity indicator (L3, L6).

Stakeholders also identified inclusive development as the strongest causal pathway (25 of 69), ahead of infrastructure-enabled growth (16) and the halal economy (14).

B.4 Prescription: Front-Loading the Ecosystem Enablers

The first prescription addresses the Limits to Growth and Growth and Underinvestment archetypes. BARMM's growth has repeatedly stalled not for want of opportunity or investor interest, but because power, logistics, certification and skills could not support production at scale. The prescription is to raise capacity ahead of demand, so that the ceiling moves before growth reaches it. Respondents agreed that capacity traps are a real constraint (mean 3.99 of 5; 74.0 percent agree).

Table 3-18. Why the weakest link sets the pace: cluster readiness and system throughput
Stage in the value chainReadiness (1–5)As share of 5Cumulative throughput

Readiness is an indicative stakeholder rating, not an econometric estimate. Source: Chapter 2, Table 2-16; BIRD Validation Survey (2026).

Two enabler tracks run in parallel from Phase 1. The hardware track (L10, L11) covers energy interconnection and renewable mini-grids, including completion of the Zamboanga–Basilan Interconnection Project; farm-to-market roads in the production corridors of Maguindanao del Sur, the SGA and Lanao del Sur; port and island logistics for Tawi-Tawi and Basilan; cold-chain nodes; and digital connectivity under the Bangsamoro e-Governance Master Plan (MICT, 2025). The software track (L9, L10) covers functional literacy and industry-aligned technical and vocational training; certifiers, laboratory analysts and investment-facilitation officers recruited and trained before demand peaks; and shorter preparation and approval times for priority projects.

The test for every Phase 1 project is not only whether it is worthwhile in itself, but which downstream investment it unlocks. Basilan illustrates the point: improved power supply and the province's declaration as free of the Abu Sayyaf Group change what its 48,366 hectares of rubber can support, from raw cup-lump sales towards processing and rubber-wood products, but only if processing, logistics and skills follow in the same sequence.

Chapter 3

B.5 Prescription: Going Below the Waterline and Architecting Collaborative Governance

The second prescription works at the deeper levels of the hierarchy. The iceberg model distinguishes visible events from the patterns, structures and mental models beneath them; intervening only at the level of events produces short-term fixes (Senge, 1990). Respondents strongly endorsed this framing (mean 4.26 of 5; 85.1 percent agree), and agreed that collaborative governance is essential to the roadmap (4.08; 80.6 percent).

Table 3-19. Interventions at each level of the iceberg
LevelWhat it looks like in BARMMIEDS response
EventsApprovals announced; budget releases; individual projects launched or delayedTrack realised investment, not only approvals; report physical as well as financial progress (L12, L6)
PatternsApprovals rising faster than realised investment; execution below target; recurring delays at the same agenciesVariance triggers and corrective plans; quarterly cluster reviews (L8, L6)
StructuresOverlapping mandates; fragmented data; ad hoc allocation; capacity gaps in new municipalities in the SGAOne facilitation network and register; cluster councils; formula-based allocation with an equity floor (L5, L4)
Mental modelsZero-sum competition for resources; value seen in raw commodities rather than processing; development equated with external funding; authority vested in individuals rather than institutionsShared regional goals through inter-provincial compacts; stewardship (khalifa) and moral governance as operating principles; "power with" rather than "power over" (L3, L2)

Collaborative governance resolves three governance traps together. Big Man dynamics are weakened by institutionalising decisions: merit-based appointments, transparent procurement and open budget data (L5, L6), and by a shift from authority exercised over others to authority exercised with them (L2). Escalation is weakened by shared superordinate goals, such as the halal hub and BIMP-EAGA integration, that make cooperation between provinces more valuable than competition (L2), and by transparent, formula-based allocation (L5). Success to the Successful is weakened by explicit equity goals and a proposed allocation floor for lagging and island areas, subject to legal design (L3, L5; Chapter 7, B3).

Section A
Section A

Strategic Alignment with the Integrated Ecosystem Development Strategy

The Integrated Ecosystem Development Strategy (IEDS), recommended in Chapter 3, operationalizes a synchronized, cluster-integrated investment pathway that treats economic growth as a function of interdependent systems rather than isolated sectoral outputs. Consequently, the metrics and Key Performance Indicator (KPI) framework for the Bangsamoro Investment Roadmap Development (BIRD) 2026–2035 must transcend traditional siloed monitoring. It must measure cross-cluster synchronization, governance operating system health, and the conversion of foundational endowments into export-ready, culturally authentic, and environmentally sustainable value (Silva, 2026; Kaplan & Norton, 1992).

This chapter establishes a calibrated, evidence-based benchmarking architecture anchored in BARMM's master plans, regulatory frameworks, and international standards. Each KPI is phased to align with the IEDS implementation timeline: Phase 1: Foundation Building (2026–2028), Phase 2: Acceleration (2029–2031), and Phase 3: Consolidation and Global Integration (2032–2035). The framework ensures that progress is measurable, comparable, and adaptive, enabling policymakers, development planners, and investors to track systemic transformation rather than incremental activity. For continuity with the draft series, many tables retain 2030 as an interim checkpoint; the formal end-of-phase gates are 2028, 2031 and 2035. Where a 2031 value is not yet defined, it must be calibrated and approved rather than interpolated silently.

The KPI framework is designed to feed directly into the Balanced Scorecard (Chapter 5), which organizes metrics across four causal perspectives: Financial, Stakeholder, Internal Process, and Learning & Growth. This chapter provides the what and how much of measurement; Chapter 5 provides the why and so what by linking each KPI to strategic objectives and causal pathways. Together, Chapters 4 and 5 form the measurement and management engine of the BIRD 2026–2035 (Kaplan & Norton, 1996; Silva, 2026).

Measurement Integrity and Data Contract. The KPI layer should be read together with the consolidated Chapter 2 diagnostic and Chapter 3 strategy architecture. The latest linked validation snapshot contains 76 consented survey responses, while the live analytics contract is analyticsVersion 2. Survey-derived SWOT diagnostics use the repository's canonical formulas: Strength RI = (Impact × Likelihood) / 5; Opportunity RI = √(Impact × Likelihood); Weakness Risk = Impact × Likelihood; and Threat VI = (Impact² × Likelihood) / 25. Missing SWOT families are treated as missing observations, not as zero scores. These diagnostics support prioritisation and learning; they do not, by themselves, constitute official administrative baselines or future targets. All numerical baselines, including values labelled “approximately”, “estimated”, “less than”, “not measured” or “baseline”, remain provisional until the named data owner confirms the source, reference period, method, geography and revisions. A target is a planning proposition until formally approved by the responsible authority.
Beyond Checklists: The Capabilities-Based Approach. Conventional ESG and development monitoring relies on checklists — counting activities completed rather than capabilities built. The BIRD KPI framework, informed by capabilities-based thinking (Beyond ESG, 2025), measures not whether a training was conducted but whether functional literacy improved; not whether a road was built but whether logistics costs declined; not whether a halal certificate was issued but whether export revenue grew. This shift from output metrics to outcome metrics is essential for tracking genuine ecosystem transformation.

KPI Architecture and Calibration Methodology

The KPI register is calibrated against the IEDS sequence and organised by indicator definition, unit, source owner, reference period, disaggregation, reporting frequency, verification status and phase milestone. SMART criteria are applied alongside data-quality and feasibility tests. The source draft proposes three portfolio dimensions—cross-cutting operating-system metrics (30%), cluster-specific metrics (45%) and benchmark alignment (25%). These percentages are proposed management weights, not externally validated measures of causal contribution. They may be used for a composite only after each constituent indicator has a documented direction of improvement, normalisation rule, missing-data policy and approval record. Until then, dashboards should show raw indicators and their status separately.

Measurement contract. Each KPI record must include: unique ID; definition; formula; unit; direction of improvement; baseline value and year; source owner; source document or dataset; collection frequency; reporting cut-off; disaggregation; validation status; 2028, 2031 and 2035 phase-gate values where approved; data-quality flag; revision history; responsible officer; and approval authority. The 2030 value may be retained for comparison with the original planning series, but it does not replace the formal Phase 2 end-point of 2031.

The calibration architecture ensures that KPIs remain responsive to IEDS synchronization requirements. Cross-cluster metrics are prioritized to prevent siloed progress from masking systemic bottlenecks. For example, tracking halal certification processing speed (Transformers cluster) in isolation would miss its direct influence on export volume (Connectors cluster) and investor retention (Stakeholder perspective). The framework explicitly maps these interdependencies, ensuring that lagging indicators in one cluster trigger diagnostic attention in connected clusters (Silva, 2026).

B.2 The Six Pareto KPIs

For executive monitoring, the BIRD framework uses six Pareto-style headline KPIs as a compact management shortlist. They should not be interpreted as a statistically established claim that exactly 80% of IEDS impact is caused by six variables; they provide a high-signal navigation layer that complements the full KPI register. These KPIs are tracked in real-time through the BIF-Net/MEL dashboard (proposed operating model) and serve as the primary navigational instruments for strategy execution. Each Pareto KPI is linked to specific Leverage Points (LP1-LP5) and Systems Archetypes, enabling rapid identification of intervention points when deviations occur (Silva, 2026).

How the six headline KPIs are calculated. (1) Annual investment approvals = sum of the formally approved values of distinct projects recorded within the reporting year; not disbursement or realised investment. (2) GRDP = the published PSA series, with annual growth calculated as (current-year ÷ previous-year − 1) × 100 using the same price basis. (3) Total exports = sum of eligible export values for the defined regional/product scope and period, with the data owner and valuation basis recorded. (4) Halal-certified MSMEs = unique MSMEs holding a valid certificate on the cut-off date; distinguish active certificates from cumulative certifications. (5) Household electrification rate = households with electricity access ÷ total eligible households × 100, using the same household definition and geography. (6) Broadband connectivity = eligible households, premises or population with the defined quality threshold of broadband access ÷ the corresponding total eligible denominator × 100. The dashboard must not mix household, premises and population denominators.
Adaptive Recalibration Protocol

To prevent the "Fixes that Fail" systems archetype, the BIRD framework employs adaptive recalibration: incentives and resource releases are conditional on enabler capacity meeting production demand thresholds. If a KPI deviates >15% from its approved trajectory, the following protocol activates:

Step 1: Alert through the dashboard only after the relevant data connector and notification rule have been tested.

Step 2: Cross-cluster diagnostic — is the deviation caused by internal cluster failure or upstream/downstream dependency?

Step 3: Leverage-point diagnosis — which of the five CLPs and relevant BSC objectives addresses the root cause?

Step 4: Trigger-based intervention — recommend resequencing, corrective action or escalation to the legally responsible decision-maker; funding changes require the applicable approval process.

Cross-Cutting Operating Systems Metrics

The IEDS positions Moral Governance, Resilience, Inclusivity, and Peace as the operational backbone of economic transformation. KPIs in this dimension measure institutional health, adaptive capacity, equitable participation, and security-investment alignment. The draft assigns these cross-cutting metrics a proposed 30% portfolio weight because they function as systemic multipliers — improvements in governance transparency, climate resilience, social inclusion, and peace directly amplify performance across all five BEIE clusters (Silva, 2026; OCM-BARMM, 2020).

C.1 Moral Governance

Moral Governance, anchored in the Bangsamoro Moral Governance Framework 2020-2035 (OCM-BARMM, 2020), is the operating system that determines whether all other clusters function effectively. The framework operationalizes Islamic ethics (khalifa stewardship), transparency, and accountability as foundational governance principles. KPIs in this dimension track the institutionalization of these principles across BARMM government operations (Silva, 2026).

The budget execution rate KPI is particularly critical because it captures the absorptive capacity constraint that has historically undermined BARMM's development. At less than 80% execution, BARMM effectively leaves 20%+ of allocated funds unspent — a pattern that constitutes both fiscal waste and lost development opportunity. The 2035 target of >90% requires systematic reform of procurement processes, human resource deployment, and inter-agency coordination. Provincial variation is significant: Maguindanao del Norte (administrative centre) likely exceeds 85% execution, while the SGA (8 newly created municipalities) may execute below 60% due to capacity constraints. The BEGMP digital platform provides real-time tracking of budget execution at provincial and municipal levels, enabling targeted capacity-building interventions (MFBM, 2025; BDP, 2023).

C.2 Resilience

Resilience metrics capture BARMM's capacity to absorb, adapt to, and recover from climate shocks, economic disruptions, and security incidents. The climate resilience dimension is particularly urgent: El Nino-induced crop losses of ₱346 million in Maguindanao del Sur (2024) and Pestalotiopsis disease infestation of 800+ hectares of rubber plantations demonstrate the vulnerability of the agricultural base that supports 32.4% of BARMM's GRDP (MENRE-BARMM, 2024; PSA-RSSO BARMM, 2025).

C.3 Inclusivity

Inclusivity metrics ensure that economic growth translates into equitable benefit distribution across provinces, genders, age groups, and marginalized communities. With poverty incidence among families at 34.8% in the first semester of 2023 (23.5% on the full-year measure, still among the highest of all regions), the lowest basic literacy of any region (81.0%) and functional literacy of 64.7% against 70.8% nationally (PSA, 2025), and significant provincial disparities (Maguindanao del Sur at 53% vs. Lanao del Sur at 31.5%), inclusivity is not merely a social objective but an economic imperative — inclusive growth generates larger markets, more productive workforces, and more stable communities (PSA, 2024; PSA-RSSO BARMM, 2024).

Peace and security metrics capture the intersection of conflict dynamics and investment climate. BARMM's post-conflict context — including Basilan's ASG-free declaration (June 2024), the Marawi rehabilitation (₱15B+), and ongoing normalization of former combatants — requires KPIs that track both security outcomes and their translation into investor confidence (OPAPRU, 2024; PIA, 2025).

Cluster-Specific Performance Indicators

Cluster KPIs are calibrated to measure throughput, value addition, market access, and financial channeling. Each indicator is explicitly linked to IEDS synchronization requirements and master plan milestones. The draft assigns these metrics a proposed 45% portfolio weight and are organized around the five BEIE clusters: Foundations (agriculture, fisheries, forestry, energy, environment), Transformers (industry, manufacturing, logistics, halal, tourism, MSMEs), Enablers (infrastructure, digital, health, education, human capital), Connectors (trade, exports, BIMP-EAGA, digital trade), and Financiers (Islamic banking, takaful, microfinance, waqf) (Silva, 2026).

D.1 Foundations Cluster

The Foundations Cluster captures BARMM's natural resource endowments — agriculture (32.4% of GRDP), fisheries, forestry, and renewable energy (75.86% mix). KPIs in this cluster measure productivity gains, post-harvest loss reduction, cooperative strengthening, renewable energy expansion, and environmental conservation. Provincial data integration is essential because each province specializes in different commodities: Basilan (rubber, 48,366 ha, 69,392 MT), Tawi-Tawi (seaweed, 40% national output), Lanao del Sur (pineapple, corn, Lake Lanao fisheries), and Maguindanao del Sur (rice, corn, coconut) (PSA-RSSO BARMM, 2024; MAFAR, 2025).

The post-harvest loss reduction KPI illustrates the cross-cluster dependency that the BIRD framework captures: reducing losses from 20-40% to 30%+ requires cold chain infrastructure (Enablers cluster), cooperative organisation (Foundations cluster), and market linkages (Connectors cluster). Basilan's 69,392 MT rubber production currently loses an estimated 25-30% value between harvest and export due to lack of processing facilities — a loss of approximately ₱400M annually that could be captured through halal-certified rubber goods manufacturing if the Transformers cluster develops concurrently (MAFAR, 2025; MTIT-BARMM, 2025).

D.2 Transformers Cluster

The Transformers Cluster measures value addition, manufacturing, and market-readiness across halal industry, tourism, MSME development, and ecozone operations. This cluster is where BARMM's foundational endowments are converted into export-ready products and services. KPIs track halal certification expansion, export value growth, tourism development, MSME formalization, and industrial locator performance (MTIT-BARMM, 2025; BEZA, 2025).

D.3 Enablers Cluster and Human Capital

The Enablers Cluster captures the physical, digital, and human infrastructure that enables all other clusters to function. This is the highest-priority cluster in IEDS Sequence A (2026-2028) because, as the systems mapping in Chapter 3-2 demonstrated, infrastructure and human capital deficits constitute the binding "Limits to Growth" constraints that stall economic transformation. The Enablers KPIs are divided into two sub-dimensions: physical/digital infrastructure and human capital development (BEGMP, 2025; TESDA-BARMM, 2025).

Human Capital as the Master Enabler: The functional literacy rate (64.7% → 75%+) is the single most important enabler KPI because it determines the absorptive capacity of all other investments. At 64.7% functional literacy, and with the lowest basic literacy of any region, BARMM cannot fully utilize digital governance platforms (BEGMP), operate complex processing machinery (Transformers), or engage with Islamic financial products (Financiers). The 15.7 percentage point improvement target requires coordinated action across DepEd (basic education), TESDA (technical skills), and MICT (digital literacy) — a cross-agency coordination challenge that the inter-agency coordination score (5.5/10 → 8/10) directly measures.

D.4 Connectors Cluster

The Connectors Cluster measures trade facilitation, export readiness, BIMP-EAGA integration, and digital trade infrastructure. This cluster becomes the priority in IEDS Sequence C (2032-2035) because market access is only valuable when production capacity (Transformers) and logistics infrastructure (Enablers) are already in place. Premature focus on Connectors without adequate Foundations, Transformers, and Enablers creates "empty corridors" — trade routes with insufficient volume to justify their cost (BIMP-EAGA, 2024; MTIT-BARMM, 2025).

D.5 Financiers Cluster

The Financiers Cluster measures the depth and reach of Islamic banking, takaful, microfinance, and waqf instruments across BARMM. With Islamic banking assets below ₱2 billion and adult financial inclusion at approximately 38% (vs. national targets of 70%+), the Financiers cluster represents both a significant gap and a transformative opportunity. Islamic finance is uniquely aligned with BARMM's identity — Shariah-compliant instruments provide culturally appropriate financial access for Muslim communities that may avoid conventional banking for religious reasons (IsDB-ICD, 2025; BSP, 2024).

International, National and Regional Benchmark Alignment

To ensure global competitiveness and policy coherence, BIRD KPIs are explicitly calibrated against four external benchmarking frameworks: OIC/SMIIC halal standards, ESG disclosure criteria, the Philippine Development Plan (PDP) 2023–2028, and the UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). This multi-layer alignment ensures that BARMM's metrics remain investable, auditable, and comparable to ASEAN and OIC member economies — critical for attracting foreign direct investment, accessing ODA and climate finance, and securing halal market recognition (SMIIC, 2021; NEDA, 2023; UNDP, 2023).

The benchmark alignment analysis reveals strategic complementarities and potential tensions. The strongest alignment is between the SDGs and PDP — both frameworks prioritize poverty reduction, education, and inclusive growth, creating a unified national-regional policy environment. The OIC/SMIIC halal standards provide a distinctive benchmark that differentiates BARMM from other Philippine regions — no other region tracks halal certification processing time or OIC accreditation status, giving BARMM a unique positioning metric for Islamic market investors.

The ESG framework adds a global investability dimension. With international investors increasingly screening for ESG compliance, BARMM's renewable energy share (75.86%, already among the highest in the Philippines), carbon credit potential (1M+ tCO2e/year target), and climate-risk screening coverage (0% → 100%) create compelling ESG narratives for green finance and climate-focused development partners. The TCFD (Task Force on Climate-Related Financial Disclosures) alignment ensures that BARMM's climate metrics meet international reporting standards, enabling access to green bonds, climate insurance, and carbon market mechanisms (MENRE-BARMM, 2024; NEDA, 2023).

Benchmark Alignment Insight: The halal certification processing time target (45-60 days → ≤21 days) directly benchmarks Malaysia's 15-day standard — the regional best practice. Achieving ≤21 days by 2035 positions BARMM as competitive within ASEAN while maintaining the quality rigor that OIC/SMIIC accreditation requires. The intermediate target of 30 days by 2030 is calibrated to be achievable given BHB capacity constraints while demonstrating progressive improvement to prospective investors. This is a "stretch but achievable" target — ambitious enough to drive institutional reform but realistic enough to maintain credibility.
KPI Composite Scoring Weights

The draft proposes three weighted dimensions for a future composite score:

Cross-Cutting OS Metrics (proposed 30%): Moral Governance, Resilience, Inclusivity, Peace & Security — systemic multiplier effect on all clusters.

Cluster-Specific Throughput (proposed 45%): Foundations, Transformers, Enablers, Connectors, Financiers — direct production and service delivery.

Benchmark Alignment (proposed 25%): alignment with OIC/SMIIC, relevant ESG disclosures, PDP and SDGs — global competitiveness and investability.

Note: Weights are calibrated to prioritize ecosystem health over isolated output maximization. A province could score highly on cluster throughput while failing on inclusivity. The proposed 30% OS weight is intended to make this trade-off visible, but it does not itself prevent inequity unless the indicator normalisation, geography, missing-data rule and approval process are implemented consistently. Until these scoring rules are approved, report the dimensions separately and do not publish a single composite as an audited measure.

Calibration Governance Rule. Baselines should be frozen only after source verification; targets should be treated as approved planning targets rather than observed facts; and any target revision should record the reason, approving authority, effective date, and affected data series. Quarterly variance review should distinguish data-quality variance, implementation variance, and external-shock variance before corrective action is assigned. This preserves comparability across the 2026–2035 horizon and prevents target drift from being mistaken for performance improvement.

Chapter Summary

Management role. Chapter 5 turns the Integrated Ecosystem Development Strategy (IEDS) in Chapter 3 into a manageable set of objectives, causal hypotheses, accountable actions and review routines. Chapter 4 remains the authority for KPI definitions, evidence rules, baseline qualification and calibration; Chapter 5 organises how that evidence informs decisions and execution.

Balanced Scorecard. The management design comprises 27 strategic objectives across four perspectives: Financial (30%), Stakeholder (25%), Internal Process (25%), and Learning & Growth (20%). These weights are a proposed management weighting scheme, not a substitute for indicator-level definitions or data quality checks.

Causal hypotheses. Five pathways connect capability-building and enabling processes to stakeholder value and economic outcomes. They express testable hypotheses, not proof that one intervention alone causes an observed change. Dependency, time-lag, external factors and unintended effects must be assessed at each review.

Phased execution. The three-phase roadmap in Chapter 3 provides the sequencing frame. The Phase 1 investment envelope of ₱35–45 billion is indicative and remains subject to project readiness, safeguards, financing confirmation and annual budget decisions. The ten actions below are a proposed management pipeline, not evidence of approved allocations or procurement commitments.

Evidence, Measurement and Governance Contract. Chapter 5 is the management layer between the strategy architecture in Chapter 3 and the KPI/calibration architecture in Chapter 4. The latest linked validation snapshot contains 76 consented survey responses; the live analytics contract is analyticsVersion 2. Survey-derived SWOT diagnostics use the canonical formulas implemented in the validation-survey analytics function: Strength RI = (Impact × Likelihood) / 5; Opportunity RI = √(Impact × Likelihood); Weakness Risk = Impact × Likelihood; and Threat VI = (Impact² × Likelihood) / 25. Missing SWOT families are treated as missing observations, not zeros. These survey diagnostics inform prioritisation, hypothesis formation and learning; they are not official regional baselines. Administrative baselines, investment approvals, GRDP, exports, poverty, infrastructure, certification, jobs and other official indicators must be verified with their authoritative data owners and documented with definitions, periods, geography, units, revision status and provenance before being adopted as formal baselines or targets. A figure in this chapter marked as a baseline or target is provisional unless this verification is recorded.

Chapter 5

A. From Strategy Map to Investment Roadmap

The Balanced Scorecard (BSC), developed by Kaplan and Norton (1992, 1996), serves as a strategic management tool that translates vision and strategy into actionable objectives across four interconnected perspectives. In the context of the Bangsamoro Investment Roadmap Development (BIRD) 2026–2035, the Balanced Scorecard functions not merely as a performance measurement system but as an investment strategy roadmap that maps causal relationships between strategic objectives.

The BSC creates a strategy map that connects intangible assets — human capital, information systems and organisational culture — to intended economic and social outcomes (Kaplan & Norton, 1996). In BIRD, the GRDP, employment and poverty figures are strategic aspirations carried forward from the roadmap, not guaranteed effects of the BSC. Chapter 4 governs their definitions and calibration; formal baselines, trajectories and targets remain provisional until verified with authoritative data owners.

"The Balanced Scorecard is not merely a performance measurement tool; it is the strategic operating system that ensures the IEDS strategy is executed with discipline, coordination, and accountability."

The BSC employs a causal hypothesis chain: Learning & Growth (enablers) → Internal Process (delivery capability) → Stakeholder (investor and community outcomes) → Financial (economic results). The proposed score weights are Financial 30%, Stakeholder 25%, Internal Process 25%, and Learning & Growth 20%. Use these weights only as a portfolio-level management convention; they do not alter Chapter 4 KPI formulas, data-quality rules, or the need to verify baseline evidence. Reviewers should test the assumed direction of causality and identify external influences, delays and possible trade-offs.

A.2 Chapter Organisation

The scorecard and its management components are presented in the following sequence:

  1. Financial Perspective (30%) — Investment mobilization, GRDP growth, export revenue, green economy revenue, Islamic finance assets, and foreign direct investment
  2. Stakeholder Perspective (25%) — Investor satisfaction, project retention, MSME certification, poverty reduction, financial inclusion, employment creation, and provincial equity
  3. Internal Process Perspective (25%) — Investment facilitation, permit processing, halal certification, infrastructure delivery, BMOA synchronization, green economy activation, and climate resilience
  4. Learning & Growth Perspective (20%) — Halal expertise, Islamic finance professionals, IPA capacity, digital innovation, functional literacy, green economy expertise, and TESDA-industry alignment

Each perspective contains strategic objectives derived from the Integrated Ecosystem Development Strategy (IEDS) in Chapter 3, with proposed measures linked to the KPI framework in Chapter 4, which remains authoritative for definitions and calibration. The chapter concludes with the Strategy Map showing causal linkages across perspectives, the Phase 1 Priority Action Plan, and BIF-Net/MEL Dashboard integration specifications.

B.2 Strategy Map Logic: Financial Perspective

The Financial Perspective objectives create an integrated value creation chain where each objective reinforces the others:

  • F1 → F2: Investment approvals provide capital for GRDP growth through direct productive capacity expansion and multiplier effects
  • F2 → public services: GRDP growth generates the tax base for public services and infrastructure reinvestment
  • F3 → F2: Export revenue brings foreign exchange that strengthens GRDP through trade multiplier effects
  • F4 → fiscal resilience: Green economy revenue diversifies revenue streams, reducing fiscal dependence on traditional sources
  • F5 → F1 + MSMEs: Islamic finance channels capital to investment approvals and MSME financing
  • F6 → F3: FDI brings technology transfer that enhances export competitiveness

C.2 Strategy Map Logic: Stakeholder Perspective

The Stakeholder Perspective creates a value delivery chain that connects investor confidence to community welfare:

  • S1 + S2 → F1: Investor satisfaction and project retention sustain investment approvals, creating a potential capital base for economic growth
  • S3 + S5 → S4: MSME empowerment through halal certification and financial inclusion enable inclusive growth, directly contributing to poverty reduction
  • S6 → S4: Quality employment creation directly lifts households out of poverty through wage income
  • S7 → S4: Provincial equity prevents the "Success to the Successful" archetype (Silva & Unsi, 2026) by testing whether investment and outcomes are distributed equitably across the applicable territorial units

The S7 objective is particularly critical in the BARMM context. The draft cites a 3.9 percentage-point inter-provincial growth disparity for 2024. Treat this as an unverified diagnostic until its calculation, geographic coverage and data owner are confirmed; any interpretation of which provinces lag must use a consistent territorial baseline. The proposed 2035 ambition is to reduce the disparity below 1.5 percentage points. Options such as infrastructure allocation criteria and provincial facilitation support should be assessed through territorial equity analysis and adopted only through the relevant budget and governance processes.

D.2 Strategy Map Logic: Internal Process Perspective

The Internal Process Perspective creates an operational excellence chain that converts intangible capabilities into tangible stakeholder outcomes:

  • P1 + P2 → S1: Streamlined business registration and permit processing directly enhance investor satisfaction by reducing time-to-operation
  • P3 → S3 + F3: Halal certification unlocks MSME empowerment and export revenue by opening OIC/SMIIC-compliant market access
  • P4 → F2: Infrastructure delivery removes binding constraints (the B1 loop ceiling identified in Chapter 2 Systems Mapping), enabling GRDP growth
  • P5 → P4: BMOA synchronization prevents agency fragmentation, improving infrastructure delivery coordination
  • P6 → F4: Green economy activation generates direct revenue from carbon credits and payment for ecosystem services
  • P7 → F2 (protection): Climate resilience protects GRDP from climate shocks, addressing the "Fixes that Fail" archetype where unprotected infrastructure investments are lost to extreme weather events

E. Learning & Growth Perspective: Intangible Assets and Capabilities

Strategic Question: "How will we sustain our ability to change, improve, and achieve our vision?"

The Learning & Growth Perspective defines the intangible assets that support value-creating internal processes. For BARMM, this includes human capital (skills and knowledge), information capital (systems and databases), and organisation capital (culture, leadership, and alignment). With a 20% weight, this foundational perspective invests in the region's capacity to execute strategy over the long term.

F. Strategy Map: Causal Linkages Across Perspectives

The Balanced Scorecard strategy map sets out causal hypotheses across the four perspectives. It proposes that capability investments (Learning & Growth) may improve delivery processes (Internal Process), which may improve investor and community outcomes (Stakeholder), contributing to economic results (Financial). It is a learning model rather than a predictive guarantee. Reviews should test assumptions against verified evidence, track external factors and time lags, and revise or retire pathways where the evidence does not support them.

F.1 Strategy Map Architecture

The strategy map operates across four hierarchical levels:

Level 1: Learning & Growth (Foundation)

  • Human Capital: L1–L7 — Halal expertise, Islamic finance professionals, IPA capacity, digital skills, literacy, green expertise, industry-aligned training
  • Information Capital: Digital systems (BEGMP), databases (BHB certification logs), MRV systems for carbon accounting
  • Organization Capital: Culture of excellence under Moral Governance, leadership alignment across BMOA, institutional memory

Level 2: Internal Process (Operations)

  • Investment Facilitation: P1–P2 — Business registration and permit processing
  • Certification & Standards: P3 — Halal certification with OIC/SMIIC accreditation
  • Infrastructure Delivery: P4 — Budget execution and project completion
  • Coordination & Governance: P5–P7 — BMOA synchronization, green economy activation, climate resilience

Level 3: Stakeholder (Value Proposition)

  • Investor Value: S1–S2 — Satisfaction and retention
  • MSME Value: S3 — Certification and market access
  • Community Value: S4–S7 — Poverty reduction, employment, financial inclusion, provincial equity

Level 4: Financial (Economic Outcomes)

  • Investment Mobilization: F1, F6 — Domestic and foreign investment approvals
  • Economic Growth: F2 — GRDP expansion
  • Revenue Diversification: F3–F5 — Exports, green economy, Islamic finance

F.2 Five Critical Causal Pathways

The strategy map sets out five proposed causal pathways linking capability objectives to intended financial outcomes. Each pathway represents a distinct theory of change with specific CLP alignments and should be reviewed against measurable intermediate outcomes. The pathways operationalise the IEDS sequencing logic in Chapter 3: build foundations first, establish enabling conditions, scale productive transformers, strengthen connectors and financing, then consolidate results. The exact sequencing of individual projects remains subject to readiness, interdependency and financing checks.

Pathway 1: Halal Economy Value Chain

L1 → P3 → S3 → F3

Halal expertise enables certification, which empowers MSMEs, driving halal export revenue. Primary CLP: LP1

Pathway 2: Infrastructure-Enabled Growth

L3 + L4 → P1 + P4 → S1 → F1 → F2

IPA capacity and digital innovation enable streamlined registration and infrastructure delivery, raising investor satisfaction and driving investment-led GRDP growth. CLPs: LP2 LP3

Pathway 3: Green Economy Monetization

L6 → P6 + P7 → F4 → F2

Green economy expertise activates carbon programmes and climate resilience, generating green revenue that contributes to GRDP. CLP: LP5

Pathway 4: Inclusive Development

L5 + L7 → S6 + S5 → S4 → F2

Functional literacy and TESDA alignment create quality employment and financial inclusion, reducing poverty and expanding the economic base. CLPs: LP1 LP4

Pathway 5: Islamic Finance Ecosystem

L2 → P3 + S5 → F5 → F1

Islamic finance professionals enable Shariah-compliant certification and financial inclusion, expanding Islamic finance assets that channel capital into new investments. CLP: LP4

G. Bangsamoro Investment Facilitation Network (BIF-Net) and MEL Dashboard

The Balanced Scorecard transforms the Integrated Ecosystem Development Strategy from a conceptual framework into an executable investment roadmap. By establishing causal linkages across four perspectives, the BSC ensures that intangible investments are explicitly linked to tangible outcomes. The Bangsamoro Investment Facilitation Network (BIF-Net) and its MEL (Monitoring, Evaluation and Learning) Dashboard serve as the operational layer that tracks, visualises, and manages BSC execution in real time.

BIF-Net: Three-View Facilitation Architecture

The proposed BIF-Net may provide three role-based views. Any Supabase Row Level Security (RLS), access model, audit logging and public-data release must be implemented and security-tested before the design is described as operational:

  • Operations View — Dashboard for authorised operators, with validated KPI updates, proposed variance alerts and territorial disaggregation where the underlying data permit
  • Executive View — Summary for authorised decision-makers, showing trends, gaps to approved trajectories and leverage-point coverage
  • Public View — Proposed, disclosure-reviewed open-data presentation with read-only access to approved investment-climate indicators

G.1 Six Pareto-Style Headline KPIs

The MEL Dashboard uses six headline KPIs as a compact management shortlist. “Pareto-style” refers only to the shortlist concept: it does not establish that these indicators account for 80% of impact or replace the complete KPI register in Chapter 4. Each KPI maps to specific BSC Financial and Stakeholder objectives and carries CLP badges for leverage point alignment:

G.4 Automated Alerting and Adaptive Management

The proposed BIF-Net operating model may use variance alerts when verified KPIs depart from an approved trajectory. The threshold must be standardised with Chapter 4 and formally adopted; this chapter uses 15% as an illustrative candidate, not an already deployed system rule. This trigger-based intervention system enables adaptive management through quarterly strategy reviews. When a KPI falls off-track:

  1. Alert Generation: An approved data workflow (automated only after implementation and testing) detects deviation using version-controlled KPI definitions and validated refresh timestamps
  2. Root Cause Analysis: BIF-Net operators drill down to identify which CLP is underperforming
  3. Intervention Trigger: The system recommends specific Phase 1 actions aligned with the affected CLP
  4. Escalation: KPI deviations persisting for two consecutive quarterly reviews are escalated to the designated accountable decision-maker under an approved governance protocol

Chapter 7 alignment and decision gates. Before an action advances from pipeline to funded implementation, apply the relevant Chapter 7 recommendations: verify the evidence owner and baseline; complete project-readiness and safeguards checks; reconcile legal mandates and approvals; test financing additionality and the proposed capital stack; assess territorial equity and investor aftercare needs; and define measurable output, outcome and risk indicators. H.1 CLP Coverage Analysis

The action pipeline maps to all five Critical Leverage Points (CLPs), but a single action may support more than one CLP. Accordingly, action counts must not be summed as though each action belongs to only one category. Costs should be attributed to the action once in the pipeline total, with a separate, explicitly documented method used for any CLP-level portfolio allocation.

Financial reconciliation. The ten indicative action-cost entries in Table 5-7 should be rechecked against their scope and currency basis before aggregation. Do not infer that their sum represents the full Phase 1 investment envelope of ₱35–45 billion. Reconcile the action pipeline with Chapter 3’s phased envelope and Chapter 6’s PAP register, identifying overlaps, multi-year costs, funding sources, approvals and annual cash requirements.

H.2 Action Tracking Requirements

Each Phase 1 action is tracked in the proposed action register or BIF-Net once implemented, using the following management requirements:

  • Gantt timeline view (2026–2028) with quarterly milestones and dependency mapping

  • Responsible party dashboard showing lead agency accountability and cross-agency coordination status
  • CLP coverage heatmap ensuring all 5 leverage points receive adequate resource allocation
  • Risk register linked to Systems Thinking archetypes from Chapter 2, with mitigation triggers
